卷一百三十九 列傳第八十九: 陸贄

Volume 139 Biographies 89: Lu Zhi

Chapter 143 of 舊唐書 ✓ Translated
← Previous Chapter
Chapter 143

1
陸贄，字敬輿，蘇州嘉興人。 父侃，溧陽令，以贄貴，贈禮部尚書。 贄少孤，特立不群，頗勤儒學。 年十八登進士第，以博學宏詞登科，授華州鄭縣尉。 罷秩，東歸省母，路由壽州，刺史張鎰有時名，贄往謁之。 鎰初不甚知，留三日，再見與語，遂大稱賞，請結忘年之契。 及辭，遺贄錢百萬，曰：「願備太夫人一日之膳。 」贄不納，唯受新茶一串而已，曰：「敢不承君厚意。 」又以書判拔萃，選授渭南縣主簿，遷監察御史。 德宗在東宮時，素知贄名，乃召為翰林學士，轉祠部員外郎。 贄性忠盡，既居近密，感人主重知，思有以效報，故政或有缺，巨細必陳，由是顧待益厚。
Lu Zhi, whose courtesy name was Jingyu, came from Jiaxing in Suzhou. His father Kan had served as magistrate of Liyang; when Zhi rose to prominence, Kan was posthumously honored as Minister of Rites. Zhi lost his father while still young. He held himself apart from others and applied himself diligently to classical learning. At eighteen he passed the jinshi examination and also qualified through the Broad Learning and Grand Phrase test, after which he was appointed county defender of Zheng in Hua Prefecture. After his term ended he traveled east to visit his mother. Passing through Shou Prefecture, he called on the prefect Zhang Yin, who was widely esteemed at the time. Yin did not think much of him at first, but after Zhi had stayed three days and they had spoken twice more, Yin came to admire him greatly and asked to become his friend despite the gap in their years. When Zhi was leaving, Yin gave him a million cash and said, "Please accept this for one day's meals for your mother." " Zhi declined the money, accepting only a single bundle of fresh tea, and said, "I would never fail to acknowledge your generous kindness." " He later passed the document-review examination with highest honors, was selected and appointed chief clerk of Weinan County, and was then promoted to investigating censor. While still heir apparent, Dezong had long known Zhi's reputation. He summoned him as a Hanlin academician and later appointed him vice director of sacrificial affairs. Zhi was loyal to the core. Once he served close to the throne and felt the emperor's deep trust, he sought every way to repay it. Whenever he saw a flaw in policy, large or small, he spoke up; the emperor's regard for him only deepened.
2
建中四年，硃泚謀逆，從駕幸奉天。 時天下叛亂，機務填委，征發指蹤，千端萬緒，一日之內，詔書數百。 贄揮翰起草，思如泉註，初若不經思慮，既成之後，莫不曲盡事情，中於機會； 胥吏簡劄不暇，同舍皆伏其能。 轉考功郎中，依前充職。 嘗啟德宗曰：「今盜遍天下，輿駕播遷，陛下宜痛自引過，以感動人心。 昔成湯以罪己勃興，楚昭以善言復國。 陛下誠能不吝改過，以言謝天下，使書詔無忌，臣雖愚陋，可以仰副聖情，庶令反側之徒，革心向化。 」德宗然之。 故奉天所下書詔，雖武夫悍卒，無不揮涕感激，多贄所為也。
In the fourth year of Jianzhong, Zhu Ci plotted rebellion, and the emperor fled with the court to Fengtian. Rebellion engulfed the empire, and state business piled up without end. Levies and orders flew in every direction; within a single day hundreds of edicts had to be drafted. Zhi drafted them at the brush; ideas poured forth like a spring. At first his drafts seemed effortless, yet when finished each one fully addressed the matter and seized the moment. The clerks could barely keep up copying his drafts, and everyone in the Hanlin office marveled at his skill. He was promoted to director of the Bureau of Appointments while continuing his Hanlin duties. He once urged Dezong, "Bandits now fill the realm and the throne is driven into exile. Your Majesty should openly blame yourself and thereby move the hearts of the people." In antiquity Cheng Tang revived his power by confessing his faults, and King Zhao of Chu restored his state by heeding good counsel. "If Your Majesty will not hesitate to amend your ways and apologize to the realm in your edicts, holding nothing back, then even someone as dull as I can help fulfill your intent, and those who waver may turn their hearts toward loyalty." " Dezong agreed. The edicts issued at Fengtian moved even rough soldiers to tears of gratitude; most of them were drafted by Zhi.
3
其年冬，議欲以新歲改元。 而卜祝之流，皆以國家數鐘百六，凡事宜有變革，以應時數。 上謂贄曰：「往年群臣請上尊號『聖神文武』四字，今緣寇難，諸事並宜改更，眾欲朕舊號之中更加一兩字，其事何如？ 」贄奏曰：「尊號之興，本非古制。 行於安泰之日，已累謙沖； 襲乎喪亂之時，尤傷事體。 今者鑾輿播越，未復宮闈，宗社震驚，尚愆禋祀，中區多梗，大憝猶存。 此乃人情向背之秋，天意去就之際，陛下宜深自懲勵，收攬群心，痛自貶損，以謝靈譴，不可近從末議，重益美名。 」帝曰：「卿所奏陳，雖理體甚切，然時運必須小有改跡，亦不可執滯，卿更思量。 」贄曰：「古之人君稱號，或稱皇稱帝，或稱王，但一字而已。 至暴秦，乃兼皇帝二字，後代因之。 及昏僻之君，乃有聖劉、天元之號。 是知人主輕重，不在自稱，崇其號無補於徽猷； 損其名不傷其德美。 然而損之有謙光稽古之善，崇之獲矜能納諂之譏，得失不侔，居然可辨。 況今時遭迍否，事屬傾危，尤宜懼思，以自貶抑。 必也俯稽術數，須有變更。 與其增美稱而失人心，不若黜舊號以祗天戒。 天時人事，理必相符，人既好謙，天亦助順。 陛下誠能斷自宸鑒，煥發德音，引咎降名，深示刻責，惟謙與順，一舉而二美從之。 」德宗從之，但改興元年號而已。
That winter the court discussed changing the reign era at the new year. Diviners and ritual specialists argued that the dynasty had entered an inauspicious cycle and that reforms were needed to align with the times. The emperor said to Zhi, "Years ago the ministers asked to give me the honorific 'Sagely, Divine, Martial, and Civil.' Now, with rebellion upon us, many say everything should change, and some want to add one or two words to my old title. What do you think?" " Zhi replied, "Honorific titles were never part of ancient practice." Even in peaceful times they burden a ruler's humility; to adopt them in the midst of disaster is still more damaging to propriety. Your carriage is still in exile, the palace unrestored, the altars unsettled, sacrifices neglected, the heartland obstructed, and the chief rebel still at large. This is the moment when the people's loyalty hangs in the balance and Heaven's favor may depart. Your Majesty should discipline yourself, win back every heart, and humble yourself before Heaven—not heed petty counsel and pile on more empty praise. " The emperor said, "Your reasoning is sound, but the times demand some outward change; we cannot be rigid. Think again." " Zhi said, "Ancient rulers called themselves Huang, Di, or Wang—a single word each." Only under the tyrannical Qin were Huang and Di combined, and later dynasties followed suit. Only muddled rulers took titles such as 'Sagely Liu' or 'Heavenly Prime.' A ruler's stature does not depend on what he calls himself; grand titles do nothing for good government; and reducing one's title does not diminish one's virtue. Humility wins the praise of antiquity, while inflation invites the charge of pride and flattery—the difference is obvious. Now, in perilous times, you should all the more reflect in fear and humble yourself. If you must bow to divination and change something, better to strip away your old title and heed Heaven's warning than add flattering words and lose the people's hearts. Heaven and humanity must align: when men love humility, Heaven aids those who yield. If Your Majesty will decide from your own judgment, speak with moral clarity, confess fault, and lower your title—one act will win both humility and Heaven's favor. " Dezong accepted his advice and changed only the era name to Xingyuan.
4
初，德宗倉皇出幸，府藏委棄，凝冽之際，士眾多寒，服禦之外，無尺縑丈帛。 及賊泚解圍，諸籓貢奉繼至，乃於奉天行在貯貢物於廊下，仍題曰「瓊林」、「大盈」二庫名。 贄諫曰：
When Dezong first fled in panic, the treasury was abandoned. In the bitter cold the troops had nothing beyond the clothes on their backs—not a scrap of silk or cloth. After Zhu Ci lifted the siege, tribute from the provinces poured in. At the Fengtian palace the gifts were stored in the corridors under the labels "Qionglin" and "Daying"—the names of two private treasuries. Zhi remonstrated:
5
「瓊林」、「大盈」，自古悉無其制，傳諸耆舊之說，皆云創自開元。 貴臣貪權，飾巧求媚，乃言：「郡邑貢賦所用，盍各區分：賦稅當委於有司，以給經用； 貢獻宜歸於天子，以奉私求。 」玄宗悅之。 新是二庫，蕩心侈欲，萌柢於茲，迨乎失邦，終以餌寇。 《記》曰：「貨悖而入，必悖而出。 」豈其效歟！
"The treasuries called Qionglin and Daying have no precedent in antiquity. Elders say they were created in the Kaiyuan reign." Greedy courtiers, seeking favor with clever words, argued that local tribute should be split: taxes ought to go to the regular offices for state expenses, while gifts should belong to the emperor for his private use. " Xuanzong was pleased. These two treasuries fed extravagant desire from the start; in the end they helped bring down the dynasty and became booty for rebels. The Record of Rites says, "Wealth gained unjustly is lost unjustly." " Was that not exactly what happened!
6
陛下嗣位之初，務遵理道，敦行儉約，斥遠貪饕。 雖內庫舊藏，未歸太府，而諸方曲獻，不入禁闈，清風肅然，海內丕變。 近以寇逆亂常，鑾輿外幸，既屬憂危之運，宜增儆勵之誠。 臣昨奉使軍營，出經行殿，忽睹右廓之下，榜列二庫之名，戄然若驚，不識所以。 何者？ 天衢尚梗，師旅方殷，痛心呻吟之聲，噢咻未息； 忠勤戰守之效，賞賚未行。 諸道貢珍，遽私別庫，萬目所視，孰能忍情？ 竊揣軍情，或生觖望，或忿形謗讟，或醜肆謳謠，頗含思亂之情，亦有悔忠之意。 是知氓俗昏鄙，識昧高卑，不可以尊極臨，而可以誠義感。
When Your Majesty first ascended the throne, you upheld right principle, practiced frugality, and kept the greedy at a distance. Although the inner treasury had not yet been merged with the public coffers, irregular gifts from the provinces no longer entered the palace, and the realm felt a refreshing change. Now rebellion has driven you into exile—a time of crisis when you should be all the more vigilant and sincere. Yesterday, on my way to the army camps, I passed the traveling palace and suddenly saw placards under the right corridor naming those two treasuries. I was shocked and could not understand why. Why? The roads are still blocked and the armies hard pressed; the wounded still groan; those who fought loyally have yet to be rewarded. Yet tribute from every circuit is set aside for private treasuries before ten thousand watching eyes. Who can bear that? I fear the troops may grow resentful, voice slander, or sing mocking songs—some already incline toward mutiny, others regret their loyalty. Common soldiers are simple and cannot be ruled by lofty display alone; they respond to sincerity and justice.
7
頃者六師初降，百物無儲，外扞兇徒，內防危堞，晝夜不息，殆將五旬。 凍餓交侵，死傷相枕，畢命同力，竟夷大艱。 良以陛下不厚其身，不私其欲，絕甘以同卒伍，輟食以啖功勞。 無猛制人而不攜，懷所感也； 無厚賞士而不怨，悉所無也。 今者攻圍已解，衣食已豐，而謗讟方興，軍情稍沮，豈不以勇夫常性，嗜貨矜功，其患難既與之同憂，而好樂不與之同利，茍異恬默，能無怨咨！ 此理之常，故不足怪。 《記》曰：「財散則民聚。 」豈其效歟！ 陛下天資英聖，見善必遷，是將化蓄怨為銜恩，反過差為至當，促殄遺寇，永垂鴻名，大聖應機，固當不俟終日。
When the imperial armies first reached Fengtian, supplies were empty. They fought the rebels outside and held the walls within, day and night, for nearly fifty days. Cold and hunger ravaged them; the dead and wounded lay piled together. They gave their all and at last overcame the crisis. This was because Your Majesty denied yourself, shared hardship with the ranks, and gave your own food to those who had earned merit. You ruled without harshness yet none deserted you, because they felt your care; and though you could not reward them richly, they did not complain, because you had nothing to give. Now the siege is lifted and supplies plentiful, yet grumbling spreads and morale falters. Brave men love reward and prize their deeds: they shared your hardship, but when fortune returns they do not share the gain. How could they not murmur in discontent? This is only human nature and nothing to wonder at. The Record says, "When wealth is dispersed, the people gather." " Will that not prove true again! Your Majesty is wise and quick to amend wrongs. You can turn stored resentment into gratitude, correct this mistake at once, destroy the remaining rebels, and win lasting renown. A sage acts when the moment demands—surely you need not wait even a day.
8
上嘉納之，令去其題署。
The emperor approved and ordered the placards removed.
9
興元元年，李懷光異志已萌，欲激怒諸軍，上表論諸軍衣糧薄，神策衣糧厚，厚薄不均，難以驅戰，意在撓沮進軍。 李晟密奏，恐其有變，上憂之，遣贄使懷光軍宣諭。 使還，贄奏事曰：
In the first year of Xingyuan, Li Huai'guang already harbored rebellious intent. He memorialized that the other armies received thin rations while the Shence troops were well supplied, claiming such inequality made campaigning impossible—his aim was to stall the advance. Li Sheng secretly warned that Huai'guang might rebel. The emperor, alarmed, sent Zhi to announce the court's will to Huai'guang's camp. On his return Zhi reported:
10
賊泚稽誅，保聚宮苑，勢窮援絕，引日偷生。 懷光總仗順之軍，乘制勝之氣，鼓行芟翦，易若摧枯。 而乃寇奔不追，師老不用，諸帥每欲進取，懷光輒沮其謀。 據茲事情，殊不可解。 陛下意在全護，委曲聽從，觀其所為，亦未知感。 若不別為規略，漸相制持，唯以姑息求安，終恐變故難測。 此誠事機危迫之秋也，故不可以尋常容易處之。
The rebel Zhu Ci awaits punishment, holed up in the palace grounds, his strength spent and aid gone, clinging to life day by day. Huai'guang commands the loyal armies and holds the advantage; a forward march would cut Zhu Ci down as easily as breaking dry wood. Yet he will not pursue the fleeing enemy, keeps the army idle, and whenever other commanders wish to advance, Huai'guang blocks them. On these facts his conduct is utterly inexplicable. Your Majesty has sought to protect him and indulged his wishes, yet he shows no gratitude. Unless you adopt another strategy and begin to restrain him, seeking peace through indulgence alone will end in unpredictable disaster. This is a moment of urgent crisis and cannot be handled as an ordinary matter.
11
今李晟奏請移軍，適遇臣銜命宣慰，懷光偶論此事，臣遂泛問所宜，懷光乃云：「李晟既欲別行，某亦都不要藉。 」臣猶慮有翻覆，因美其軍強盛。 懷光大自矜誇，轉有輕晟之意。 臣又從容問云：「昨發離行在之日，未知有此商量； 今日從此卻回，或恐聖旨顧問，事之可否，決定何如？ 」懷光已肆輕言，不可中變，遂云：「恩命許去，事亦無妨。 」要約再三，非不詳審，雖欲追悔，固難為詞。 伏望即以李晟表出付中書，敕下依奏，別賜懷光手詔，示以移軍事由。 其手詔大意云：「昨得李晟奏，請移軍城東以分賊勢。 朕緣未知利害，本欲委卿商量，適會陸贄從彼宣慰回，雲見卿論敘軍情，語及於此，仍言許去，事亦無妨，遂敕本軍允其所請。 卿宜授以謀略，分路夾攻，務使葉齊，克平寇孽。 」如此詞婉而直，理當而明，雖蓄異端，何由起怨？
Li Sheng has asked to move his army. On my mission I happened to hear Huai'guang mention it, and I asked what he thought. He said, "If Li Sheng wants to march separately, I need none of his help." " Still fearing he might change his mind, I praised the strength of his troops. Huai'guang swelled with pride and showed contempt for Li Sheng. I then asked calmly, "When I left the palace yesterday this move had not been discussed; on my return His Majesty may ask whether this is approved. What is your decision?" " Having spoken rashly, he could not take it back, and said, "If the Emperor permits it, there is no harm." " He repeated his assent clearly; even if he regrets it now, he cannot easily withdraw. I beg Your Majesty to send Li Sheng's memorial to the Secretariat, approve the move by edict, and separately send Huai'guang a handwritten edict explaining the transfer. The edict might read: "Yesterday Li Sheng memorialized asking to move his army east of the city to divide the rebel force." Not knowing the pros and cons, I meant to consult you. Lu Zhi has just returned from your camp and reports that in discussing the army you agreed the move would do no harm. I have therefore ordered Li Sheng's request granted." Give him your plan, attack from two sides, and together destroy the rebels." " Such wording would be courteous yet firm; even if he harbors ill will, how could he complain?
12
臣初奉使諭旨，本緣糧料不均，偶屬移軍，事相諧會。 又幸懷光詭對，且無阻絕之言，機宜合並。 若有幽贊，一失其便，後何可追，幸垂裁察！
My mission was originally about unequal rations; the question of moving troops arose by chance and fell out favorably. Fortunately Huai'guang answered evasively and did not refuse outright—the opportunity aligns. With Heaven's hidden aid, if we miss this chance it cannot be recovered. I beg Your Majesty to decide at once!
13
德宗初望懷光回意破賊，故晟屢奏移軍不許； 及贄縷陳懷光反狀，乃可晟之奏，遂移軍東渭橋。 而鄜坊節度李建徽、神策行營陽惠元猶在咸陽，贄慮懷光並建徽等軍，又奏曰：
At first Dezong hoped Huai'guang would repent and destroy the rebels, so he had repeatedly refused Li Sheng's request to move; but after Zhi detailed Huai'guang's rebellious conduct, he approved Li Sheng's memorial, and the army moved to East Wei Bridge. Li Jianhui, military commissioner of Fufang, and Yang Huiyuan of the Shence mobile camp were still at Xianyang. Fearing that Huai'guang would absorb Jianhui's forces and the others, Lu Zhi submitted another memorial:
14
懷光當管師徒，足以獨制兇寇，逗留未進，抑有他由。 所患太強，不資傍助。 比者又遣李晟、李建徽、陽惠元三節度之眾附麗其營，無益成功，只憂生事。 何則？ 四軍懸壘，群帥異心，論勢力則懸絕高卑，據職名則不相統屬。 懷光輕晟等兵微位下，而忿其制不從心。 晟等疑懷光養寇蓄奸，而怨其事多陵己。 端居則互防飛謗，欲戰則遞恐分功，齟齬不和，嫌釁遂構，俾之同處，必不兩全。 強者惡積而後亡，弱者勢危而先覆，覆亡之禍，翹足可期。 舊寇未平，新患方起，憂嘆所切，實堪疚心。 太上消慝於未萌，其次救失於始兆，況乎事情已露，禍難垂成，委而不謀，何以制亂？ 李晟見機慮變，先請移軍就東，建徽、惠元，勢轉孤弱，為其吞噬，理在必然。 他日雖有良圖，亦恐不能自拔，拯其危急，唯在此時。 今因李晟願行，便遣合軍同往，托言晟兵素少，慮為賊泚所邀，藉此兩軍，叠為掎角。 仍先諭旨，密使促裝，詔書至營，即日進路。 懷光意雖不欲，然亦計無所施。 是謂先人有奪人之心，疾雷不及掩耳者也。
Huai'guang commanded sufficient forces to subdue the rebels on his own; if he lingered without advancing, there must have been some other reason. The concern was that he was too powerful to need outside help. Yet the court had recently sent the three commissioners Li Sheng, Li Jianhui, and Yang Huiyuan to camp alongside him. That would not aid victory; it would only create new problems. Why is that? Four armies were encamped apart, and their commanders were divided in mind. In strength they stood far apart in rank; in title none was subordinate to the others. Huai'guang despised Sheng and the others for their weaker forces and lower rank, and resented that he could not fully command them. Sheng and his colleagues suspected Huai'guang of deliberately sheltering the enemy and nursing treachery, and resented his repeated encroachments on their authority. In camp they would watch each other and whisper accusations; in battle each would fear the others would share the credit. Friction bred suspicion, and if forced to remain together, neither side could come out intact. The stronger party would accumulate enmity and eventually be destroyed; the weaker would fall first in their precarious position. Disaster could be expected at any moment. The old enemy was not yet subdued, and a new threat was rising—an anxiety that truly wrung the heart. The best course is to dispel evil before it takes root; the next is to correct a fault at the first warning. When the danger is already visible and disaster near at hand, how can we fail to act and still expect to master the turmoil? Li Sheng, reading the situation, had already asked to move east. Once isolated, Jianhui and Huiyuan would inevitably be absorbed by Huai'guang. Even later a good plan might come too late to save them. Only now can their danger be averted. Take Li Sheng's willingness to move as pretext, and order Jianhui and Huiyuan to march with him, claiming that Sheng's forces are too small and might be cut off by Zhu Ci, so that the two armies could support each other as pincers. The Emperor should first send secret orders to prepare for departure, so that when the edict reaches camp the armies march the same day. Huai'guang would dislike it, but he would have no way to prevent it. That would be to strike first, like thunder before one can cover one's ears.
15
夫制軍馭將，所貴見情，離合疾徐，各有宜適。 當離者合之則召亂，當合者離之則寡功； 當疾而徐則失機，當徐而疾則漏策。 得其要，契其時，然後舉無敗謀，措無危勢。 而今者屯兵而不肯為用，聚將而罔能葉心，自為鯨鯢，變在朝夕。 留之不足以相制，徒長歷階； 析之各競於擅能，或成勛績。 事有必應，斷無可疑。
In commanding armies and generals, one must read their disposition; when to unite, when to divide, when to hurry or delay—each has its proper time. Uniting those who should be kept apart invites chaos; separating those who should fight together yields little success; acting too slowly when speed is needed loses opportunity; acting too hastily when deliberation is needed spoils the plan. Only by grasping the essentials and acting at the right moment can every move succeed without dangerous entanglements. Now troops are massed but refuse to serve, and generals gathered but unable to trust one another—they have become monsters in their own right, and revolt may come at any hour. Keeping them together will not keep them in check; it will only let danger grow step by step; separating them would let each command independently and perhaps win merit. This course must be taken; there can be no doubt.
16
德宗曰：「卿之所料極善。 然李晟移軍，懷光心已惆悵，若更遣建徽、惠元就東，則使得為詞。 且俟旬時。 」晟至東渭橋，不旬日，懷光果奪兩節度兵，建徽單騎遁而獲免，惠元中路被執，害之。 報至行在，人情大恐。 翌日，移幸山南。 贄練達兵機，率如此類。
Dezong said, "Your assessment is excellent. But Li Sheng has already moved his army, and Huai'guang is already displeased. If we also send Jianhui and Huiyuan east, we would only give him a pretext. Let us wait a few more days. " Li Sheng reached East Wei Bridge; within ten days Huai'guang seized the forces of the two commissioners. Jianhui escaped alone on horseback; Huiyuan was captured en route and killed. When news reached the imperial camp, panic spread. The next day Dezong fled to Shannan. Lu Zhi's grasp of military affairs was generally of this caliber.
17
二月，從幸梁州，轉諫議大夫，依前充學士。 先是，鳳翔衙將李楚琳乘涇師之亂，殺節度使張鎰，歸款硃泚。 及奉天解圍，楚琳遣使貢奉，時方艱阻，不獲已，命為鳳翔節度使。 然德宗忿其弒逆，心不能容，才至漢中，欲令渾瑊代為節度。 贄諫曰：「楚琳之罪，固不容誅，但以乘輿未復，大憝猶存，勤王之師，悉在畿內，急宣速告，晷刻是爭。 商嶺則道迂且遙，駱谷復為賊所扼，僅通王命，唯在褒斜，此路若又阻艱，南北便成隔絕。 以諸鎮危疑之勢，居二逆誘脅之中，恟々群情，各懷向背。 賊勝則往，我勝則來，其間事機，不容差跌。 儻楚琳發憾，公肆猖狂，南塞要沖，東延巨猾，則我咽喉梗而心膂分矣，其勢豈不病哉！ 」上釋然開悟，乃善待楚琳使，優詔安慰其心。
In the second month he accompanied the emperor to Liang Prefecture, was promoted to remonstrance and discussion grandee, and continued as Hanlin academician. Earlier, Fengxiang garrison officer Li Chulin had taken advantage of the mutiny of the Jingzhou forces to kill Zhang Yin, military commissioner of Fengxiang, and submit to Zhu Ci. After the siege of Fengtian was lifted, Chulin sent envoys with tribute. Because the court was in dire straits, it had no choice but to appoint him military commissioner of Fengxiang. Dezong, however, could not forgive Chulin for murdering his commander. As soon as he reached Hanzhong, he wanted Hun Jian to replace him as military commissioner. Lu Zhi remonstrated: "Chulin's crime surely deserves death, but the Emperor has not yet returned to the capital, the chief rebel still lives, and the armies that rallied to the throne are all still in the vicinity. Every moment counts for urgent dispatches. The Shangling road is long and roundabout, and Luogu is again held by the enemy. Baoxie is the only route by which imperial orders can pass. If that too is blocked, north and south will be cut off from each other. The regional commands are wavering, caught between two rebel powers that tempt and threaten them. Public sentiment is unsettled, and loyalties are divided. They side with whoever wins. At such a moment there is no room for error. If Chulin takes offense and rebels openly, he will block the southern gateway and link up with the great rebel in the east. Our lifeline will be choked and our forces split—is that not a grave peril? " The emperor saw the point and treated Chulin's envoys kindly, sending a reassuring edict to mollify him.
18
德宗至梁，欲以谷口已北從臣賜號曰「奉天定難功臣」，谷口已南隨扈者曰「元從功臣」，不選朝官，一例俱賜。 贄奏曰：「破賊扞難，武臣之效。 至如宮闈近侍，班列員僚，但馳走從行而已，忽與介胄奮命之士，俱號功臣，伏恐武臣憤惋。 」乃止。
When Dezong reached Liang, he proposed to grant the title "Meritorious Officials Who Pacified the Crisis at Fengtian" to followers north of Gukou, and "Original Follow Meritorious Officials" to those south of Gukou, without distinguishing court officials—all would receive the honor alike. Lu Zhi memorialized: "Defeating rebels and bearing hardship are the deeds of military men. Palace attendants and civil officials merely followed on the march. To call them meritorious officials alongside armored warriors who risked their lives would surely anger the military. " Dezong dropped the plan.
19
李晟既收京城，遣中使宣付翰林院具錄先散失宮人名字，令草詔賜渾瑊，遣於奉天尋訪，以得為限，仍量與資糧送赴行在。 贄不時奉詔，進狀論之曰：
After Li Sheng recovered the capital, he sent an imperial envoy to the Hanlin Academy with orders to compile a list of palace women lost in the chaos, draft an edict for Hun Jian, and dispatch him to Fengtian to search for them and send any found, with supplies, to the imperial camp. Lu Zhi did not immediately comply. Instead he submitted a memorial arguing against the order:
20
頃以理道乖錯，禍亂薦鐘，陛下思咎懼災，裕人罪己，屢降大號，誓將更新。 天下之人，垂涕相賀，懲忿釋怨，煦仁戴明，畢力同心，共平多難。 止土崩於絕岸，收版蕩於橫流，殄寇清都，不失舊物。 實由陛下至誠動於天地，深悔感於神人，故得百靈降康，兆庶歸德。 茍不如此，自古何嘗有捐棄宮闕，失守宗祧，繼逆於赴難之師，再遷於蒙塵之日，不逾半歲，而復興大業者乎！
Not long ago, because governance had gone astray, calamity piled upon calamity. Your Majesty reflected on your faults, showed mercy to the people, and took blame upon yourself, issuing great proclamations again and again and vowing a new beginning. People across the realm wept with joy, set aside old grievances, and warmed to your benevolence and wisdom, joining with one heart to overcome the crisis. You halted the empire's collapse at the brink, gathered the realm from the flood, destroyed the rebels, and recovered the capital without losing the dynasty's heritage. This was truly because Your Majesty's sincerity moved Heaven and Earth and your deep repentance touched gods and men, so that all spirits brought peace and the people returned to loyalty. Had it not been so, when in all history has an emperor who abandoned his palace, lost his ancestral shrines, fled with the army in crisis, and moved his court twice in disgrace restored the dynasty in less than half a year?
21
今渠魁始平，法駕將返，近自郊甸，遠周寰瀛，百役疲瘵之氓，重戰傷殘之卒，皆忍死扶病，傾耳聳肩，想聞德聲，翹望聖澤。 陛下固當感上天悔禍之眷，荷列祖垂裕之休，念將士鋒刃之殃，湣黎元塗炭之酷。 以致寇為戒，以居上為危，以務理為憂，以復宮為急。 損之又損，尚懼汰侈之易滋； 艱之惟艱，猶患戒慎之難久。 謀始盡善，克終已稀； 始而不謀，終則何有！ 夫以內人為號，蓋是中壺末流。 天子之尊，富有宮掖，如此等輩，固繁有徒，但恐傷多，豈憂乏使！ 翦除元惡，曾未浹辰，奔賀往來，道途如織。 何必自虧君德，首訪婦人，又令資裝速赴行在！ 萬目閱視，眾口流傳，恐非所以答慶賴之心，副惟新之望也。
Now the chief rebel has just been subdued and the imperial procession is about to return. From the capital suburbs to the farthest provinces, exhausted commoners and battle-worn soldiers—all who have endured death and sickness strain to hear your virtuous rule and await your benevolent care. Your Majesty should be grateful for Heaven's mercy in turning aside disaster, mindful of the blessings left by your ancestors, considerate of the soldiers' wounds, and compassionate toward the people's suffering. Let the rebellion be a warning, high station a source of caution, good governance your chief concern, and the restoration of the palace your most urgent task. Even after repeated retrenchment, one must still guard against the return of luxury; even in hardship one must still fear that caution cannot long endure. Many begin well; few finish well; and if one does not plan from the start, what can one hope for at the end? Making palace women the first concern belongs to the least important affairs of the inner court. The Son of Heaven's household is already full of attendants; there are more than enough. The concern is having too many, not too few! The chief villain was eliminated less than ten days ago, and congratulatory traffic already fills the roads. Why diminish your own moral authority by making women your first concern and ordering supplies to rush them to the imperial camp? With all eyes watching and all tongues wagging, I fear this will not answer the people's hopes for celebration nor fulfill their expectation of renewal.
22
夫事有先後，義有重輕，重者宜先，輕者宜後。 武王克殷，有未及下車而為之者，有下車而為之者，蓋美其不失先後之宜也。 自翠華播越，萬姓靡依，清廟震驚，三時乏祀，當今所務，莫大於斯。 誠宜速遣大臣，馳傳先往，迎復神主，修整郊壇，展禋享之儀，申告謝之意。 然後吊恤死義，慰犒有功，綏輯黎蒸，優問耆耋。 安定反側，寬宥脅從； 宣暢郁堙，褒獎忠直； 官失職之士，復廢業之人。 是皆宜先，不可後也。 至如崇飾服器，繕緝殿臺，備耳目之娛，選巾櫛之侍，是皆宜後，不可先也。
Affairs have their order, and duties their priorities. The weighty should come first, the light afterward. When King Wu conquered the Shang, some tasks he performed before even stepping down from his chariot and some afterward—because he honored the proper order of priorities. Since the Emperor was driven into exile, the people have been left adrift; the ancestral temple was shaken and sacrifices have been neglected for seasons. Nothing today is more urgent than this. Your Majesty should swiftly send senior ministers ahead by relay to recover the spirit tablets, restore the suburban altars, perform the sacrificial rites, and offer thanks to Heaven. Then mourn the loyal dead, reward the meritorious, reassure the people, and inquire after the elderly. Pacify those who wavered, pardon those forced into rebellion; give voice to suppressed grievances, and honor the loyal and upright; restore officials displaced from office and people driven from their livelihoods. All of these should come first—not last. Adorning robes and vessels, repairing palaces, providing diversions for eyes and ears, and selecting personal attendants—all of these should come later, not first.
23
散失內人，已經累月，既當離亂之際，必為將士所私。 其人若稍有知，不求當自陳獻； 其人若甚無識，求之適使憂虞。 自因寇亂喪亡，頗有大於此者，一聞搜索，懷懼必多； 余孽尚繁，群情未一，因而善撫，猶恐危疑，若又懼之，於何不有！ 昔人所以掩絕纓而飲盜馬者，豈必忘其情愛，蓋知為君之體然也。 以小妨大，明者不為。 天下固多褻人，何必獨在於此。 所令撰賜渾瑊詔書，未敢順旨。
The lost palace women have been missing for months. In the chaos of rebellion, they were surely taken privately by officers and soldiers. If they have any sense, they will come forward on their own without being searched for; if they lack understanding, searching for them will only create alarm. In the chaos many have suffered losses far greater than this. Once a search is announced, countless people will be afraid; rebel remnants are still numerous and public sentiment is not yet settled. Even with gentle handling people remain uneasy; if you frighten them further, what mischief might follow? The ancients who covered a loose bridle and let a thief drink from their horse did not forget their own property—they understood what it means to be a ruler. The wise do not let small matters obstruct great ones. There are servants enough in the realm; why fix on these alone? As for the edict you ordered me to draft for Hun Jian, I dare not comply.
24
帝遂不降詔，但遣使而已。
The emperor then issued no edict and sent only an envoy.
25
德宗還京，轉中書舍人，學士如故。 初，贄受張鎰知，得居內職； 及鎰為盧杞所排，贄常憂惴； 及杞貶黜，始敢上書言事。 德宗好文，益深顧遇。 奉天解圍後，德宗言及違離宗廟，嗚咽流涕曰：「致寇之由，實朕之過。 」贄亦流涕而對曰：「臣思致今日之患者，群臣之罪也。 」贄意蓋為盧杞、趙贊等也。 上欲掩杞之失，則曰：「雖朕德薄，致茲禍亂，亦運數前定，事不由人。 」贄又極言杞等罪狀，上雖貌從，心頗不說。 吳通微兄弟俱在翰林，亦承德宗寵遇，文章才器不迨贄； 而能交結權幸，共短贄於上前。 故劉從一、姜公輔自卑品蒼黃之中，皆登輔相； 而贄為朋黨所擠，同職害其能，加以言事激切，動失上之歡心，故久之不為輔相。 其於議論應對，明練理體，敷陳剖判，下筆如神，當時名流，無不推挹。
When Dezong returned to the capital, Lu Zhi was promoted to secretariat drafter while remaining Hanlin academician. Lu Zhi had originally owed his inner-court appointment to Zhang Yin's patronage; when Yin was ousted by Lu Qi, Lu Zhi lived in constant anxiety; only after Qi was demoted did he dare to speak openly on state affairs. Dezong loved literary talent and favored him all the more. After the siege of Fengtian was lifted, Dezong spoke of having been torn from the ancestral temple and wept, saying, "The rebellion was truly my fault. " Lu Zhi wept in reply, "Your Majesty, I believe today's calamity was the fault of your ministers. " He had Lu Qi, Zhao Zan, and others in mind. The emperor, wishing to shield Qi, said, "Though my virtue was insufficient and brought this disaster, it was also predestined fate—not the work of men. " Lu Zhi again pressed the crimes of Qi and his allies. Dezong assented outwardly but was displeased at heart. Wu Tongwei and his brother, both in the Hanlin Academy, also enjoyed Dezong's favor, though their literary talent fell short of Lu Zhi's; but they cultivated ties with powerful favorites and together slandered Lu Zhi before the throne. Thus Liu Congyi and Jiang Gongfu rose from humble stations to become chief ministers; while Lu Zhi was squeezed out by factions, envied by colleagues for his talent, and—because his remonstrances were sharp and often offended the emperor—for long was never made chief minister. In debate and reply he was lucid on principle, his expositions incisive, his pen seemingly inspired; every leading figure of the age admired him without exception.
26
貞元初，李抱真入朝，從容奏曰：「陛下幸奉天、山南時，赦書至山東，宣諭之時，士卒無不感泣。 臣即時見人情如此，知賊不足平也。」
Early in the Zhenyuan era, Li Baozhen came to court and said calmly, "When Your Majesty was at Fengtian and in the south, the amnesty reached Shandong; as it was read aloud, not a soldier failed to weep. I saw the mood of the men at once and knew the rebels could never be crushed."
27
時贄母韋氏在江東，上遣中使迎至京師，搢紳榮之。 俄丁母憂，東歸洛陽，寓居嵩山豐樂寺。 籓鎮賻贈及別陳餉遺，一無所取。 與韋臯布衣時相善，唯西川致遺，奏而受之。 贄父初葬蘇州，至是欲合葬。 上遣中使護其柩車至洛，其禮遇如此。 免喪，權知兵部侍郎，依前充學士。 申謝日，贄伏地而泣，德宗為之改容敘慰。 恩遇既隆，中外屬意為輔弼，而宰相竇參素忌贄，贄亦短參之所為，言參黷貨，由是與參不平。
Lu Zhi's mother, Lady Wei, was then in the lower Yangzi region; the emperor sent palace envoys to bring her to the capital, an honor the court took as a mark of distinction. Before long he entered mourning for his mother, went east to Luoyang, and took lodging at Fengle Temple on Mount Song. He accepted none of the condolence gifts sent by the regional commanders, nor any other offerings pressed upon him. He had been close to Wei Gao since their days as commoners; only gifts from Xichuan did he accept, and then only after memorializing the throne and receiving permission. Lu Zhi's father had first been buried in Suzhou; he now wished to reinter him beside his mother. The emperor sent palace envoys to escort the coffin to Luoyang — such was the honor shown him. When his mourning ended, he was named acting Vice Minister of War while retaining his post as Hanlin academician. On the day he presented his thanks, Lu Zhi prostrated himself in tears; Dezong's face softened and he spoke words of consolation. His favor now ran so high that court and country alike looked to him as a future chief minister; yet the chief minister Dou Can had long resented him, and Lu Zhi in turn denounced Can's conduct as corrupt — so the two were estranged.
28
七年，罷學士，正拜兵部侍郎，知貢舉。 時崔元翰、梁肅文藝冠時，贄輸心於肅。 肅與元翰推薦藝實之士，升第之日，雖眾望不愜，然一歲選士，才十四五，數年之內，居臺省清近者十余人。
In the seventh year he left the Hanlin Academy, was formally appointed Vice Minister of War, and given charge of the civil examinations. Cui Yuanhan and Liang Su then stood at the head of the age in letters; Lu Zhi gave Liang Su his full trust. Liang Su and Yuanhan put forward men of real ability; when the results were announced, public opinion was disappointed, for only fourteen or fifteen candidates passed that year — yet within a few years more than ten of them held prestigious posts in the Secretariat and Censorate.
29
八年四月，竇參得罪，以贄為中書侍郎、門下同平章事。 贄久為邪黨所擠，困而得位，意在不負恩獎，悉心報國，以天下事為己任。 上即位之初，用楊炎、盧杞秉政，樹立朋黨，排擯良善，卒致天下沸騰，鑾輿奔播。 懲是之失，貞元已後，雖立輔臣，至於小官除擬，上必再三詳問，久之方下。 及贄知政事，請許臺省長官自薦屬官，仍保任之，事有曠敗，兼坐舉主。 上許之，俄又宣旨曰：「外議云：『諸司所舉，多引用親黨，兼通賂遺，不得實才。 』此法行之非便，今後卿等宜自選擇，勿用諸司延薦。 」贄論奏曰：
In the fourth month of the eighth year Dou Can fell from power, and Lu Zhi was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Associate Chief Minister. Lu Zhi, long blocked by hostile factions, had won office only after great struggle; he meant to repay the emperor's favor, serve the realm with all his heart, and treat the affairs of the empire as his own burden. At the start of his reign the emperor had entrusted power to Yang Yan and Lu Qi, who built factions, drove out the worthy, and in the end brought the realm to uproar and the court itself to flight. Chastened by that disaster, Dezong after the Zhenyuan era would question even the appointment of minor officials again and again before an order finally issued. Once Lu Zhi entered the government, he asked that heads of the Secretariat and Censorate be permitted to nominate their own subordinates under personal guarantee — if an appointee failed in office, the nominator would share the penalty. The emperor agreed; but soon he issued a new order: "There is talk abroad that the offices' nominees are mostly kin and cronies, that bribes pass hands, and that true talent is not found. This policy will not do. Hereafter you ministers must choose for yourselves and not rely on nominations from the departments.'" " Lu Zhi memorialized in reply:
30
臣實頑鄙，一無所堪，猥蒙任使，待罪宰相。 雖懷竊位之懼，且乏知人之明，自揣庸虛，終難上報。 唯知廣求才之路，使賢者各以匯征； 啟至公之門，令職司皆得自達。 既蒙允許，即宜宣行。 南宮舉人，才至十數，或非臺省舊吏，則是使府佐僚，累經薦延，多歷事任。 論其資望，既不愧於班行； 考其行能，又未聞於闕敗。 遽以騰口，上煩聖聰，道之難行，亦可知矣！
I am dull and unworthy, fit for nothing, yet I have undeservedly been placed among the chief ministers, holding office in fear of failure. I fear I hold a post beyond my merit and lack the discernment to know men; knowing my own inadequacy, I can scarcely hope to repay Your Majesty's trust. All I know is to widen the roads by which talent may be found, so that the worthy may be summoned from every quarter; and open the gates of impartial selection, so that every office may bring forward its own candidates. Your Majesty has already approved this policy; it ought now to be put into effect. The examination candidates numbered scarcely a dozen; some were veterans of the Secretariat and Censorate, others staff of commissioner offices — all repeatedly promoted, all tested in real service. By rank and reputation they were unexceptionable among their peers; and in conduct and competence nothing had been heard against them. Yet on mere rumor alone Your Majesty's ear has been troubled — from this one may see how hard it is to put good policy into practice!
31
陛下勤求理道，務徇物情，因謂舉薦非宜，復委宰臣揀擇。 其為崇任輔弼，博采輿詞，可謂聖德之盛者。 然於委任責成之道，聽言考實之方，閑邪存誠，猶恐有闕。 陛下既納臣言而用之，旋聞橫議而止之，於臣謀不責成，於橫議不考實，此乃謀失者得以辭其罪，議曲者得以肆其誣。 率是而行，觸類而長，固無必定之計，亦無必實之言。 計不定則理道難成，言不實則小人得誌。 國家之病，常必由之。 昔齊桓公問管仲害霸之事，對曰：「得賢不能任，害霸也； 用而不能終，害霸也； 與賢人謀事，而與小人議之，害霸也。 」為小人者，不必悉懷險诐，故覆邦家。 蓋以其意性回邪，趣向狹促，以沮議為出眾，以自異為不群，趨近利而昧遠圖，效小信而傷大道，況又言行難保，恣其非心者乎！
Your Majesty earnestly seeks good government and wishes to heed public sentiment; hearing that nomination was improper, you have again entrusted selection to the chief ministers. In honoring your ministers and heeding broad counsel, Your Majesty shows the greatness of a sage ruler. Yet in the matter of entrusting responsibility and holding men to account, of hearing counsel and testing its truth — in guarding against deceit and keeping faith with the upright — I fear something is still lacking. Your Majesty accepted my proposal and then, on hearing reckless criticism, set it aside — holding my plan to no account while giving no scrutiny to the critics. Thus those whose counsel fails may excuse their failure, and the dishonest may slander at will. If this pattern continues, category by category, there will be no firm policy and no word that can be trusted. Without settled policy good government cannot be achieved; without truth in counsel petty men prevail. The afflictions of the state have again and again sprung from just such causes. Once Duke Huan of Qi asked Guan Zhong what destroys hegemony. He answered, "To find worthy men and fail to use them destroys hegemony; to use them but not see the matter through destroys hegemony; to take counsel with worthy men and then debate it with petty men destroys hegemony." " Petty men need not all be treacherous schemers bent on ruin; rather, their natures are twisted and cramped: they make obstruction their distinction, contrariness their pride; they grasp at immediate gain and lose sight of the larger design, offer petty proofs of loyalty and wound the greater good — and when words and deeds cannot be trusted, what limit is there to their malice?
32
伏以宰輔，常制不過數人，人之所知，固有限極，不有遍諳諸士，備閱群才。 若令悉命群官，理須展轉詢訪，是則變公舉為私薦，易明易攵為暗投。 儻如議者之言，所舉多有情故，舉於君上，且未絕私； 薦於宰臣，安肯無詐！ 失人之弊，必又甚焉。 所以承前命官，罕有不涉私謗，雖則秉鈞不一，或自行情，亦由私訪所親，轉為所賣。 其弊非遠，聖鑒明知。 今又將徇浮言，專任宰臣除吏，宰臣不遍諳識，踵前須訪於人。 若訪親朋，則是悔其覆車，不易故轍； 若訪於朝列，則是求其私薦，不如公舉之愈也。 二者利害，惟陛下更詳擇焉。 恐不如委任長官，慎揀僚屬，所揀既少，所求亦精，得賢有鑒識之名，失實當暗謬之責。 人之常性，莫不愛身，況於臺省長官，皆是當朝華選，孰肯徇私妄舉，以傷名取責者耶！ 所謂臺省長官，即僕射、尚書、左右丞、侍郎及御史大夫、中丞是也。 陛下比擇輔相，多亦出於其中。 今之宰臣，則往日臺省長官也； 今之臺省長官，乃將來之宰臣也，但是職名暫異，固非行業頓殊。 豈有為長官之時不能舉一二屬吏，居宰臣之位則可擇千百具僚，物議悠悠，其惑斯甚。
Chief ministers are by custom only a few in number; human knowledge has its limits — no minister can know every candidate or review all talent himself. If ministers must appoint every official themselves, they will necessarily rely on roundabout inquiry — turning open nomination into private favor and transparent selection into back-room dealing. If, as the critics claim, nominations are tainted by personal ties, then even nomination to the throne has not eliminated private interest; and recommendation to a chief minister — how could fraud be absent! The harm of appointing the wrong men would be greater still. That is why past appointments have so often drawn charges of favoritism: though chief ministers differ in character and some act from private motive, the root cause is private inquiry among one's own circle — and being misled by those one trusts. This evil is no distant matter; Your Majesty's clear sight already knows it. Now, yielding again to loose talk, you would leave all appointments to the chief ministers; unable to know every candidate, they must as before consult others. If they consult kin and friends, you repeat the old mistake without changing course; if they consult within the court, they seek private recommendations — which is worse than open nomination. Between these two courses, the harm and the benefit — I ask Your Majesty to weigh them again with care. Surely it would be better to entrust department heads to choose their own staffs carefully — fewer nominees, higher standards; success would bring credit for discernment, failure would bring blame for error. All men naturally cherish their reputations — and these department heads are the court's finest appointments; who among them would risk his name with reckless favoritism! By department heads I mean the Grand Counselors, Ministers, Vice Directors, Vice Ministers, Censor-in-Chief, and Vice Censor-in-Chief. Your Majesty has lately chosen most of your chief ministers from these same ranks. Today's chief ministers were yesterday's department heads; today's department heads are tomorrow's chief ministers — the titles differ for a time, but their character and capacity are not suddenly transformed. How can the same men who, as department heads, could nominate only a handful of subordinates suddenly, as chief ministers, be trusted to choose hundreds of officials? Public murmuring shows how deep the confusion runs.
33
夫求才貴廣，考課貴精。 求廣在於各舉所知，長吏之薦擇是也； 貴精在於按名責實，宰臣之序進是也。 往者則天太后踐祚臨朝，欲收人心，尤務拔擢，弘委任之意，開汲引之門，進用不疑，求訪無倦，非但人得薦士，亦許自舉其才。 所薦必行，所舉輒試，其於選士之道，豈不傷於容易哉！ 而課責既嚴，進退皆速，不肖者旋黜，才能者驟升，是以當代謂知人之明，累朝賴多士之用。 此乃近於求才貴廣，考課貴精之效也。
In seeking talent, breadth matters; in testing performance, precision matters. Breadth comes when each man recommends those he knows — that is the role of department heads; precision comes when names are matched to deeds and responsibility enforced — that is the role of chief ministers. When Empress Wu held the throne, eager to win loyalty, she promoted men with special vigor — broad delegation, open recruitment, appointment without hesitation, search without rest; not only might others recommend talent, men might recommend themselves. Every nominee was appointed, every appointee promptly tested — was not her method of selection perhaps too lenient! Yet because accountability was strict and promotion and dismissal swift, the unworthy were quickly removed and the able quickly advanced — so her age was praised for discernment, and later reigns benefited from the abundance of talent she produced. This was close to the ideal of broad recruitment joined to rigorous assessment.
34
陛下誕膺寶歷，思致理平，雖好賢之心，有逾於前哲，而得人之盛，未迨於往時。 蓋由賞鑒獨任於聖聰，搜擇頗難於公舉，仍啟登延之路，罕施練核之方。 遂使先進者漸益雕訛，後來者不相接續，施一令則謗沮互起，用一人則瘡磐立成。 此乃失於選才太精，制法不一之患也。 則天舉用之法，傷易而得人； 陛下慎揀之規，太精而失士。 陛下選任宰相，必異於庶官； 精擇長官，必愈於末品。 及至宰相獻規，長吏薦士，陛下即但納橫議，不稽始謀。 是乃任以重者輕其言，待以輕者重其事，且又不辨所毀之虛實，不校所試之短長。 人之多言，何所不至，是將使人無所措其手足，豈獨選任之道失其端而已乎！
Your Majesty has inherited the throne and seeks good order; though your love of talent exceeds that of earlier rulers, you have not yet matched past ages in gathering able men. This is because selection rests too much on the emperor's personal judgment, open nomination has been made difficult, the door to office stands open, yet rigorous testing is rarely applied. Those promoted early have grown ever more corrupt, new talent fails to follow in their stead; every order provokes mutual slander, every appointment breeds fresh trouble. This is the harm of selecting talent too narrowly and governing by inconsistent rules. Empress Wu's method, though perhaps too lenient, did produce able men; Your Majesty's rule of cautious selection is so strict that talent is lost. Your Majesty rightly treats the choice of chief ministers differently from lesser appointments; and the careful selection of department heads with even greater care than low officials is also right. Yet when chief ministers offer policy and department heads nominate talent, Your Majesty hears only reckless criticism and does not weigh the original proposal. Thus you treat weighty advisers lightly and light matters heavily — and you do not test the truth of slander, nor weigh the success or failure of those appointed. When rumor runs free, nothing is beyond its reach; men will not know where to turn — and the damage will extend far beyond the selection of officials alone!
35
上雖嘉其所陳，長官薦士之詔，竟追寢之。
The emperor praised his argument, but the edict permitting department heads to nominate subordinates was withdrawn in the end.
36
國朝舊制，吏部選人，每年調集。 自乾元已後，屬宿兵於野。 歲或兇荒，遂三年一置選。 由是選人停擁，其數猥多，文書不接，真偽難辨，吏緣為奸，註授乖濫，而有十年不得調者。 贄奏吏部分內外官員為三分，計闕集人，每年置選。 故選司之弊，十去七八，天下稱之。
Under the old system of the dynasty, the Ministry of Personnel convened candidates for assignment every year. After the Qianyuan era, troops were kept under field garrison. In years of famine and hardship, examinations were held only once every three years. Candidates therefore accumulated in vast numbers; records fell out of sequence, credentials could not be verified, clerks exploited the confusion, and assignments grew arbitrary — some men waited ten years without a posting. Lu Zhi proposed that the Ministry divide civil and military vacancies into three categories, tally the backlog, and restore annual selection. The abuses of the selection office were thereby reduced by seven or eight tenths, and the realm applauded the reform.
37
贄與賈耽、盧邁、趙憬同知政事，百司有所申覆，皆更讓不言可否。 舊例，宰臣當旬，秉筆決事，每十日一易，贄請準故事，令秉筆者以應之。 又以河隴陷蕃已來，西北邊常以重兵守備，謂之防秋，皆河南、江淮諸鎮之軍也，更番往來，疲於戍役。 贄以中原之兵，不習邊事，及扞虜戰賊，多有敗衄，又苦邊將名目太多，諸軍統制不一，緩急無以應敵，乃上疏論其事曰：
Lu Zhi served with Jia Dan, Lu Mai, and Zhao Jing as associate chief ministers; when offices submitted business for decision, each deferred to the others and none would rule yea or nay. By custom the chief minister on weekly rotation held the brush and decided affairs, the duty changing every ten days; Lu Zhi asked that precedent be restored so that the officer holding the brush would answer for decisions. He also noted that since Hexi and Longyou had fallen to Tibet, the northwest frontier had been held by heavy garrisons in what was called autumn defense — troops drawn from the Henan and Jiang-Huai regions, rotated in endless relays, worn down by frontier service. Central troops, Lu Zhi argued, were unused to frontier warfare and often suffered defeat against barbarians and rebels; frontier commands were too fragmented and armies lacked unified control, so that in crisis they could not respond effectively. He therefore memorialized on the matter, saying:
38
臣歷觀前代書史，皆謂鎮撫四夷，宰相之任，不揆闇劣，屢敢上言。 誠以備邊禦戎，國家之重事； 理兵足食，備禦之大經。 兵不治則無可用之師，食不足則無可固之地。 理兵在制置得所，足食在斂導有方。 陛下幸聽愚言，先務積谷，人無加賦，官不費財，坐致邊儲，數逾百萬。 諸鎮收糴，今已向終，分貯軍城，用防艱急，縱有寇戎之患，必無乏絕之憂。 守此成規，以為永制，常收冗費，益贍邊農，則更經二年，可積十萬人三歲之糧矣。 足食之原粗立，理兵之術未精，敢議籌量，庶備采擇。
Reading the histories of past ages, I find that pacifying the frontier peoples has always been the chief minister's charge; unworthy though I am, I have ventured to speak on it repeatedly. Frontier defense is indeed a weighty matter for the state; and ordering the armies and filling the granaries is the great foundation of defense. Without disciplined armies there are no forces fit for use; without adequate provisions no territory can be held. Discipline depends on proper disposition of forces; provisions depend on wise methods of collection and distribution. Your Majesty has graciously heeded my counsel and made grain accumulation the first priority — without new taxes on the people or waste of public funds — so that frontier stores now exceed a million measures. The commanderies' grain purchases are nearly complete; stores are being distributed to garrison towns against emergency — even if barbarian raids come, there need be no fear of shortage. If this policy is kept as permanent rule, and surplus expenditures are redirected to support frontier agriculture, within two more years stores sufficient for three years' supply to a hundred thousand men could be accumulated. The foundation for adequate provisions is roughly in place; the methods for ordering the armies are not yet perfected — I venture these calculations in hope that Your Majesty may find something worth adopting.
39
伏以戎狄為患，自古有之，其於制禦之方，得失之論，備存史籍，可得而言。 大抵尊即序者，則曰「非德無以化要荒」，曾莫知威不立，則德不能馴也。 樂武威者，則曰「非兵無以服兇獷」，曾莫知德不修，則兵不可恃也。 務和親者，則曰「要結可以睦鄰好」，曾莫知我結之而彼復解也。 美長城者，則曰「設險可以固邦國而扞寇仇」，曾莫知力不足，兵不堪，則險之不能有也。 尚薄伐者，則曰「驅遏可以禁侵暴而省征徭，」曾莫知兵不銳，壘不完，則遏之不能勝，驅之不能去也。 議邊之要，略盡於斯，雖互相譏評，然各有偏駁。 聽一家之說，則例理可征； 考歷代所行，則成敗異效。 是由執常理以禦其不常之勢，徇所見而昧於所遇之時。
I respectfully observe that the nomadic peoples of the frontier have been a menace since ancient times. Historical records preserve full accounts of how to control and repel them, and of the debates over what succeeds and what fails — and these may still instruct us today. As a rule, those who champion moral suasion declare that only virtue can transform the far periphery — yet they fail to grasp that without established authority, virtue alone cannot bring wild lands to heel. Those who exult in military might insist that only force can subdue the fierce and unruly — yet they never see that without moral cultivation, arms alone cannot be trusted. Those committed to marriage alliances argue that treaty bonds can keep peace with neighboring peoples — yet they never reckon with how quickly such bonds are tied only to be broken again. Those who admire the Great Wall claim that fortified barriers can secure the realm and hold off invaders — yet they never consider that if power is too weak and armies too thin, no barrier can be held. Those who favor limited punitive expeditions say that driving the enemy back can check raids and spare the people heavy taxes and corvée — yet they never see that if troops lack edge and fortifications are incomplete, blocking fails and driving them off proves impossible. The main points of frontier policy debate are largely covered here. Though each camp mocks the other, every position is partial and incomplete. Heed any single school of thought, and its precedents and logic seem compelling; but examine what successive dynasties actually did, and success and failure tell a different story. The reason is that men cling to fixed principles against shifting circumstances, and follow what they have seen while blind to the age they actually face.
40
夫中夏有盛衰，夷狄有強弱，事機有利害，措置有安危，故無必定之規，亦無長勝之法。 夏後以序戎而聖化茂，古公以避狄而王業興； 周城朔方而獫狁攘，秦築臨洮而宗社覆； 漢武討匈奴而貽悔，太宗征突厥而致安； 文、景約和親而不能弭患於當年，宣、元弘撫納而足以保寧於累葉。 蓋以中夏之盛衰異勢，夷狄之強弱異時，事機之利害異情，措置之安危異便。 知其事而不度其時則敗，附其時而不失其稱則成。 形變不同，胡可專一！
The heartland waxes and wanes; the barbarians grow strong and grow weak; circumstances bring advantage and disadvantage; policy brings safety and peril. There is therefore no fixed rule, and no strategy that always wins. Yu of Xia brought the Rong into order, and sage rule flourished; Lord Tai fled the Di, and his royal enterprise took root; Zhou fortified Shuofang, and the Xianyun raided unchecked; Qin built walls at Lintao, and the dynasty fell; Emperor Wu of Han pursued the Xiongnu to exhaustion and left regret behind; Emperor Taizong campaigned against the Turks and brought the realm peace; Emperors Wen and Jing relied on marriage alliances yet could not still the troubles of their own age; Emperors Xuan and Yuan pursued conciliation and acceptance, and secured peace for generations. For the heartland's rise and fall follow different circumstances; barbarian strength and weakness shift with the times; the calculus of opportunity changes with each crisis; and what makes policy safe or perilous depends on how well it fits the moment. To know the right policy but misread the moment is to fail; to align with the moment without abandoning what is fitting is to succeed. Conditions shift without cease — how can any one method suffice!
41
夫以中國強盛，夷狄衰微，而能屈膝稱臣，歸心受制，拒之則阻其向化，威之則類於殺降，安得不存而撫之，即而序之也？ 又如中國強盛，夷狄衰微，而尚棄信奸盟，蔑恩肆毒，諭之不變，責之不懲，安得不取亂推亡，息人固境也？ 其有遇中國喪亡之弊，當夷狄強盛之時，圖之則彼釁未萌，禦之則我力不足，安得不卑詞降禮，約好通和，啖之以親，紓其交禍？ 縱不必信，且無大侵，雖非禦戎之善經，蓋時事亦有不得已也。 儻或夷夏之勢，強弱適同，撫之不寧，威之不靖； 力足以自保，不足以出攻，得不設險以固軍，訓師以待寇，來則薄伐以遏其深入，去則攘斥而戒於遠追？ 雖為安邊之令圖，蓋勢力亦有不得不然也。 故夏之即序，周之於攘，太宗之翦亂，皆乘其時而善用其勢也。 古公之避狄，文、景之和親，神堯之降禮，皆順其時而不失其稱也。 秦皇之長城，漢武之窮討，皆知其事而不度其時者也。 向若遇孔熾之勢，行即序之方，則見侮而不從矣！ 乘可取之資，懷畏避之誌，則失機而養寇矣！ 有攘卻之力，用和親之謀，則示弱而勞費矣！ 當降屈之時，務翦伐之略，則召禍而危殆矣！ 故曰：知其事而不度其時則敗，附其時而不失其稱則成。 是無必定之規，亦無長勝之法，得失著效，不其然歟！ 至於察安危之大情，計成敗之大數，百代之不變易者，蓋有之矣。 其要在於失人肆欲則必蹶，任人從眾則必全，此乃古今所同，而物理之所壹也。
When the empire is strong and the barbarians weak, and they come kneeling as subjects with hearts turned toward submission — to reject them blocks their conversion to civilization; to terrorize them is little better than slaughtering the surrendered. How then can the court fail to preserve, soothe, and bring them into order? Again: when the empire is strong and the barbarians weak, yet they break faith, spurn alliances, despise kindness, and unleash cruelty — when persuasion fails and punishment avails nothing — how can the court fail to exploit their disorder, hasten their collapse, give the people rest, and secure the frontier? When the empire is in decline and the barbarians are ascendant — to plot against them before their provocation has ripened is premature; to resist them outright exceeds our strength. What choice remains but humble words and lowered ceremony, covenants of friendship, overtures of peace, enticements of kinship, and every means to avert mutual ruin? Even when such overtures cannot be fully trusted and no great invasion is imminent, this is not ideal frontier policy — yet there are moments when no better course is possible. When barbarian and Chinese strength are evenly matched, conciliation brings no lasting peace and intimidation brings no lasting calm; when strength suffices only to defend and not to strike outward, must the court not fortify defenses, drill the army, meet incursions with limited punitive strikes to block deep penetration, and when the enemy withdraws drive them off while refraining from reckless pursuit? Though this is the soundest plan for securing the frontier, there are times when power itself leaves no alternative. Thus the Xia policy of orderly submission, the Zhou policy of active repulse, and Taizong's suppression of rebellion all seized their moment and wielded circumstance to advantage. Lord Tai's flight from the Di, the marriage alliances of Wen and Jing, and Gaozu's lowered ceremony all conformed to their times without abandoning propriety. The First Emperor's Great Wall and Emperor Wu's relentless campaigns both understood the policy but misread the moment. Had moral ordering been attempted when the enemy was at its most rampant, the court would have been mocked and the barbarians would not have submitted! To hold the advantage yet shrink from action is to forfeit opportunity and nurture the enemy! To possess the strength to drive the enemy back yet resort to marriage alliances is to show weakness and squander treasure! To pursue aggressive campaigns when the court must bow and submit is to invite disaster and court destruction! Hence the maxim: to know the right policy but misread the moment is to fail; to align with the moment without abandoning what is fitting is to succeed. There is no fixed rule and no eternally victorious strategy — outcomes prove the point. Is this not plainly so? Yet in discerning the deeper truth of safety and peril, and reckoning the larger pattern of success and failure, there may be principles that hold across the ages. The essential lesson is this: a ruler who alienates the people and indulges his desires will surely fall; one who employs the worthy and heeds broad counsel will surely endure. This truth is unchanged from antiquity to the present — it is the one constant in the nature of affairs.
42
國家自祿山構亂、河隴用兵以來，肅宗中興，撤邊備以靖中邦，借外威以寧內難。 於是吐蕃乘釁，吞噬無厭； 回紇矜功，憑陵亦甚。 中國不遑振旅，四十余年。 使傷耗遺氓，竭力蠶織，西輸賄幣，北償馬資，尚不足塞其煩言，滿其驕誌。 復乃遠征士馬，列戍疆陲，猶不能遏其奔沖，止其侵侮。 小入則驅略黎庶，深入則震驚邦畿。 時有議安邊策者，多務於所難而忽於所易，勉於所短而略於所長。 遂使所易所長者，行之而其要不精； 所難所短者，圖之而其功靡就。 憂患未弭，職斯之由。
Since An Lushan's rebellion and the wars in Hexi and Longyou, the court — even after Emperor Suzong restored the dynasty — has withdrawn frontier defenses to pacify the heartland and borrowed foreign military power to quell internal strife. Tibet seized the opening and swallowed territory without end; the Uyghurs flaunted their contributions, and their arrogance knew little bounds. For more than forty years the empire has lacked the strength to rebuild its armies. The surviving populace has been drained dry, taxed to the limit of silk production, sending tribute westward and paying for horses northward — yet still unable to silence their complaints or satisfy their pride. Even when troops were dispatched on distant campaigns and garrisons lined the frontier, the court still could not halt their raids or stop their incursions. Minor raids plundered the countryside; major incursions shook the capital itself. Those who debated frontier policy at the time mostly pursued the hard course while neglecting the easy, and strained at their weaknesses while ignoring their strengths. Thus the easy and advantageous measures, when attempted, were never executed with precision; while the difficult and ill-suited ones, when pursued, never came to fruition. That troubles remain unabated — this is the reason.
43
夫制敵行師，必量事勢，勢有難易，事有先後。 力大而敵脆，則先其所難，是謂奪人之心，暫勞而永逸者也； 力寡而敵堅，則先其所易，是謂固國之本，觀釁而後動者也。 頃屬多故，人勞未瘳，而欲廣發師徒，深踐寇境，復其侵地，攻其堅城，前有勝負未必之虞，後有饋運不繼之患。 儻或撓敗，適所以啟戎心而挫國威，以此為安邊之謀，可謂不量事勢而務於所難矣！
To subdue enemies and move armies, one must weigh circumstances. Circumstances differ in difficulty; priorities must be ordered. When one's strength is great and the enemy weak, strike first at what is hardest for him — this means seizing the initiative; brief exertion for lasting peace; when one's strength is limited and the enemy formidable, begin with what is easiest — this means securing the foundations of the state; watch for openings before moving. In recent years turmoil has been unceasing and the people are not yet recovered — yet some propose to mobilize vast armies, penetrate deep into enemy territory, recover lost lands, and assault fortified cities. Ahead lies uncertain victory; behind, the peril of broken supply lines. Should such campaigns fail, they would only embolden the barbarians and shatter the empire's prestige. To call this frontier policy is to ignore circumstances while pursuing the hardest course imaginable!
44
天之授者，有分事，無全功； 地之產者，有物宜，無兼利。 是以五方之俗，長短各殊。 長者不可逾，短者不可企； 勉所短而敵其所長必殆，用所長而乘其所短必安。 強者，乃以水草為邑居，以射獵供飲茹，多馬而尤便馳突，輕生而不恥敗亡，此戎狄之所長也。 戎狄之所長，乃中國之所短； 而欲益兵蒐乘，角力爭驅，交鋒原野之間，決命尋常之內，以此為禦寇之術，可謂勉所短而校其所長矣！ 務所難，勉所短，勞費百倍，終於無成。 雖果成之，不挫則廢，豈不以越天授而違地產，虧時勢以反物宜者哉！
Heaven assigns each people its portion — not every gift in full measure; Earth endows each land with what suits it — not every advantage combined. Hence the peoples of the four quarters differ in what they do well and what they do poorly. Strengths cannot be surpassed by force; weaknesses cannot be wished away; to strain at weakness against the enemy's strength is to court disaster; to wield strength against the enemy's weakness is to secure safety. The nomads live by pasture and water, sustain themselves by hunting; they keep many horses and excel at sudden cavalry charges; they hold life cheap and do not fear defeat or death — these are the barbarians' strengths. What the barbarians do well is precisely what China does poorly; yet to mass infantry, gather chariots, and meet them in open country for a contest of raw force and speed — to call this frontier defense is to strain at weakness and compete on the enemy's own terms! Pursue the hard course, strain at weakness — and labor and expense multiply a hundredfold while success never comes. Even if such efforts succeed, they collapse unless constantly reinforced — for they defy Heaven's apportionment, violate Earth's natural endowment, and run counter to the fitness of things and the logic of the times!
45
將欲去危就安，息費從省，在慎守所易，精用所長而已。 若乃擇將吏以撫寧眾庶，修紀律以訓齊師徒，耀德以佐威，能邇以柔遠； 禁侵抄之暴以彰吾信，抑攻取之議以安戎心； 彼求和則善待而勿與結盟，彼為寇則嚴備而不務報復，此當今之所易也。 賤力而貴智，惡殺而好生，輕利而重人，忍小以全大，安其居而後動，俟其時而後行。 是以修封疆，守要害，塹蹊隧，壘軍營，謹禁防，明斥候，務農以足食，練卒以蓄威，非萬全不謀，非百克不鬥。 寇小至則張聲勢以遏其入，寇大至則謀其人以邀其歸； 據險以乘之，多方以誤之。 使其勇無所加，眾無所用； 掠則靡獲，攻則不能； 進有腹背受敵之虞，退有首尾難救之患，所謂乘其弊，不戰而屈人之兵，此中國之所長也。 我之所長，乃戎狄之所短； 我之所易，乃戎狄之所難。 以長制短，則用力寡而見功多； 以易敵難，則財不匱而事速就。 舍此不務，而反為所乘，斯謂倒持戈矛，以钅尊授寇者也！ 今則皆務之矣，猶且守封未固，寇戎未懲者，其病在於謀無定用，眾無適從。 所任不必才，才者不必任； 所聞不必實，實者不必聞； 所信不必誠，誠者不必信； 所行不必當，當者未必行。 故令措置乖方，課責虧度； 財匱於兵眾，力分於將多，怨生於不均，機失於遙制。 臣請為陛下粗陳六者之失，惟明主慎聽而熟察之：
To move from peril toward safety, and from waste toward thrift, the answer lies in steadfastly holding what is easy and skillfully deploying what we do best — nothing more. Choose capable generals and officials to govern the people; enforce discipline to drill the armies; let virtue reinforce authority and competence at home win trust abroad; forbid predatory raids to demonstrate good faith; restrain talk of conquest to reassure the barbarians; when they sue for peace, receive them generously but bind them with no formal alliance; when they raid, fortify defenses but seek no vengeance — these are the measures readily at hand today. Esteem strategy over brute force; abhor killing and cherish life; prize people over profit; endure small losses to secure great gains; secure one's position before acting; wait for the right moment before moving. Thus: repair the frontier, hold key passes, trench roads and defiles, build fortified camps, tighten patrols, post clear scouts, promote farming to fill granaries, drill troops to build deterrence — plan nothing without full security; fight only when victory is virtually assured. When raids are small, display strength to block entry; when raids are large, target their leaders to cut off retreat; hold advantageous ground against them; employ varied stratagems to confound them. Render their valor useless and their numbers impotent; let plunder yield no spoils and assault meet no success; advance, and they face enemies on every side; retreat, and they cannot save themselves — this is what it means to exploit their weakness and defeat their armies without battle: China's own strength. What we do well is precisely what the barbarians do poorly; what comes easily to us is hard for them. Wield strength against weakness, and little effort yields great results; take the easy path against their difficulty, and treasury and manpower are spared while success comes swiftly. To neglect this and instead play to the enemy's advantage is to hold one's weapons backward and hand the blade to the foe! Today all these measures are nominally pursued, yet the frontier remains unsecured and the barbarians undeterred — because policy lacks consistent application and no one knows which course to follow. Those in office are not always capable; the capable are not always in office; what reaches the throne is not always true; what is true does not always reach the throne; those trusted are not always loyal; the loyal are not always trusted; what is done is not always right; what is right is not always done. Hence policies are misdirected and accountability fails; The treasury is drained by excessive troop numbers; force is scattered among too many commanders; resentment breeds from unfair treatment; and timely response is lost to distant micromanagement. Your subject begs leave to outline for Your Majesty the six fundamental failures — may the wise sovereign hear them with care and weigh them with full attention:
46
臣聞工欲善其事，必先利其器； 武欲勝其敵，必先練其兵。 練兵之中，所用復異。 用之於救急，則權以紓難； 用之於暫敵，則緩以應機。 故事有便宜，而不拘常制； 謀有奇詭，而不徇眾情。 進退死生，唯將所命，此所謂攻討之兵也！ 用之於屯戍，則事資可久； 勢異從權，非物理所愜不寧，非人情所欲不固。 夫人情者，利焉則勸，習焉則安，保親戚則樂生，顧家業則忘死，故可以理術馭，不可以法制驅，此所謂鎮守之兵也。 夫欲備封疆，禦戎狄，非一朝一夕之事，固當選鎮守之兵以置焉。 古之善選置者，必量其性習，辨其土宜，察其伎能，知其欲惡。 用其力而不違其性，齊其俗而不易其宜； 引其善而不責其所不能，禁其非而不處其所不欲。 而又類其紀伍，安其室家，然後能使之樂其居，定其誌，奮其氣勢，結其恩情。 撫之以惠，則感而不驕； 臨之以威，則肅而不怨。 靡督課而人自為用，弛禁防而眾自不攜。 故出則足兵，居則足食，守則固，戰則強。 其術無他，便於人情而已矣！ 今者散征士卒，分戍邊陲，更代往來，以為守備。 是則不量性習，不辨土宜，邀其所不能，強其所不欲。 求廣其數而不考其用，將致其力而不察其情，斯可以為羽衛之儀，而無益於備禦之實也。 何者？ 窮邊之地，千里蕭條，寒風裂膚，驚沙慘目； 與豺狼為鄰伍，以戰鬥為嬉遊； 晝則荷戈而耕，夜則倚烽而覘； 日有剽害之慮，永無休暇之娛，地惡人勤，於斯為甚！ 自非生於其域，習於其風，幼而睹焉，長而安焉，不見樂土而遷焉，則罕能寧其居而狎其敵也。 關東之地，百物阜殷，從軍之徒，尤被優養。 慣於溫飽，狎於歡康，比諸邊隅，若異天地。 聞絕塞荒陬之苦，則辛酸動容； 聆強蕃勁虜之名，則懾駭奪氣。 而乃使之去親族，舍園廬，甘其所辛酸，抗其所懾駭，將冀為用，不亦疏乎！ 矧又有休代之期，無統帥之馭，資奉若驕子，姑息如倩人，進不邀之以成功，退不處之以嚴憲。 其來也鹹負得色，其止也莫有固心，屈指計歸，張頤待飼。 僥倖者猶患還期之賒緩，常念戎醜之充斥； 王師挫傷，則將乘其亂離，布路東潰，情誌且爾，得之奚為？ 平居則殫耗資儲以奉浮冗之眾，臨難則拔棄城鎮以搖遠近之心，其弊豈惟無益哉！ 固亦將有所撓也。 復有抵犯刑禁，謫徙軍城，意欲增戶實邊，兼令展效自贖。 既是無良之類，且加懷土之情，思亂幸災，又甚戍卒。 適足煩於防衛，諒無望於功庸，雖前代時或行之，固非良算之可遵者也。 復有擁旄之帥，身不臨邊，但分偏師，俾守疆場。 大抵軍中壯銳，元戎例選自隨，委其疲羸，乃配諸鎮。 節將既居內地，精兵祗備紀綱，遂令守要禦沖，常在寡弱之輩。 寇戎每至，乃勢不支，入壘者才足閉關，在野者悉遭劫執，恣其芟蹂，盡其搜驅。 比及都府聞知，虜已克獲旋返。 且安邊之本，所切在兵，理兵若斯，可謂措置乖方矣！
Your subject has heard that a craftsman who wishes to do fine work must first sharpen his tools; a commander who wishes to defeat the enemy must first drill his troops. Yet even among trained troops, their uses differ. Troops deployed for emergency relief rely on expedient measures to resolve crisis; troops deployed against a passing threat rely on flexible timing to seize opportunity. Affairs admit expedient action, unconstrained by ordinary rules; plans may require unorthodox stratagems, undeterred by popular opinion. Advance, retreat, life, and death — all at the general's command. These are the troops of offensive campaign! Troops assigned to garrison duty must be suited to long service; circumstances vary and policy must adapt — what runs against nature cannot endure; what the soldiers do not willingly accept cannot hold. Human nature responds to reward and settles into routine; soldiers fight gladly when their families are protected, and hold the line when their livelihoods are secure — they may be guided by reason, but cannot be driven by coercion alone. These are garrison troops. Securing the frontier against barbarian incursion is no short-term undertaking; it requires troops specifically chosen and stationed for garrison duty. Ancient masters of recruitment weighed each man's temperament and habits, matched him to suitable terrain, assessed his skills, and understood his inclinations. They deployed men's strength without violating their nature, harmonized their customs without forcing them into unsuitable roles; Encourage what they do well without faulting what they cannot do; restrain what is wrong without forcing what they reject. Group them with suitable comrades, secure their families — only then will they find contentment in their posts, hold steady purpose, fight with full spirit, and forge genuine loyalty. Treat them with kindness, and they will feel gratitude without growing arrogant; Govern them with firm authority, and they will stand in awe without nursing resentment. Without constant supervision, men apply themselves willingly; with relaxed restrictions, the ranks hold together without desertion. Deploy them and the army is sufficient; station them and supplies hold; hold a position and the defense is solid; enter battle and the force is formidable. The secret is nothing other than working with human nature — that is all! Today men are conscripted from every district, split into detachments for frontier garrison duty, rotated in and out on relay tours — and this is called border defense. Nothing is weighed of temperament or custom, nothing matched to local conditions — men are asked to do what they cannot and forced to accept what they reject. Numbers are expanded without testing fitness for use; strength is summoned without reading men's hearts. Such a system may suffice for ceremonial guard duty, but it cannot meet the real demands of frontier defense. Why is this so? The far frontier is a thousand li of desolation — biting winds flay the skin, whipping sand stings the eyes; wolves and jackals are one's nearest neighbors, and combat is the daily diversion; by day they farm with weapons in hand; by night they stand watch at the beacon towers; each day brings fear of raid and slaughter, never a moment's rest — in harshness of terrain and severity of labor, nothing surpasses it! Unless a man is native to such country, reared in its ways, raised from childhood in its hardships and never tempted elsewhere by gentler lands, he can scarcely settle contentedly or grow accustomed to facing the enemy. East of the passes all goods abound, and soldiers there enjoy especially generous provisions. Accustomed to comfort and plenty, they know only ease and pleasure — compared with the borderlands, it might be another world. Mention the miseries of blocked passes and barren frontiers, and their faces twist with distress; speak the names of powerful tribes and fierce enemies, and terror drains the courage from their veins. Yet these same men are sent from their families, from their homes, to endure what appalls them and face what terrifies them — and we expect them to serve effectively. How misplaced is that hope! To make matters worse: rotation schedules promise release but no commander truly governs them; provisions are lavished like on favored sons while discipline is lax as with hired labor; no reward awaits success in the field, no penalty follows failure in retreat. On arrival they swagger as if winning a prize; once posted they hold no firm loyalty — counting days till rotation, mouths open waiting to be fed. Even the fortunate fret that rotation comes too slowly, while constantly brooding on the enemy hordes abroad; If the imperial army suffers defeat, they will seize the moment of confusion and scatter eastward in flight — with hearts and minds like these, what good are they? In peacetime they drain the treasury feeding a useless host; in crisis they abandon fortresses and shake confidence near and far — the harm goes far beyond mere uselessness! It actively undermines the defense as well. Criminals condemned to frontier garrison are sent to swell border populations and redeem themselves through service. These are men of bad character to begin with, further burdened with homesickness — they pray for chaos and welcome disaster — worse even than ordinary garrison troops. They burden the defenders without yielding any military gain — though earlier dynasties tried this at times, it is no sound policy to repeat. Then there are commanders with imperial banners who never go to the border themselves, sending only partial detachments to hold the line. As a rule, the strongest troops stay with the commanding general; the worn and weak are farmed out to the border posts. With the commander safe inland, his crack troops reserved for parade and protocol, the vital passes are always left to thin, weak detachments. When raiders strike, the garrison cannot hold — those who make it inside barely shut the gates; those caught outside are seized wholesale, fields ravaged, people rounded up and driven away. By the time headquarters learns of the attack, the enemy has taken what they came for and withdrawn. Securing the frontier depends above all on the army — and to manage troops thus is to misdirect policy entirely!
47
夫賞以存勸，罰以示懲，勸以懋有庸，懲以威不恪。 故賞罰之於馭眾也，猶繩墨之於曲直，權衡之揣重輕，輗軏之所以行車，銜勒之所以服馬也。 馭眾而不用賞罰，則善惡相混而能否莫殊； 用之而不當功過，則奸妄寵榮而忠實擯抑。 夫如是，若聰明可衒，律度無章，則用與不用，其弊一也。 自頃權移於下，柄失於朝，將之號令，既鮮克行之於軍，國之典章，又不能施之於將，務相遵養，茍度歲時。 欲賞一有功，翻慮無功者反側； 欲罰一有罪，復慮同惡者憂虞。 罪以隱忍而不彰，功以嫌疑而不賞，姑息之道，乃至於斯。 故使忘身效節者，獲誚於等夷； 率眾先登者，取怨於士卒； 僨軍蹙國者，不懷於愧畏； 緩救失期者，自以為智能。 褒貶既闕而不行，稱毀復紛然相亂，人雖欲善，誰為言之？ 況又公忠者，直己而不求於人，反罹困厄； 敗撓者，行私而茍媚於眾，例獲優崇。 此義士所以痛心，勇夫所以解體也。 又有遇敵而所守不固，陳謀而其效靡成； 將帥則以資糧不足為詞，有司復以供給無闕為解。 既相執證，理合辨明，朝廷每為含糊，未嘗窮究曲直。 措理者吞聲而靡訴，誣善者罔上而不慚。 馭眾若斯，可謂課責虧度矣！
Rewards exist to encourage merit; punishments to deter wrongdoing — the one to honor achievement, the other to intimidate the disobedient. In command of men, reward and punishment are what the carpenter's line is to straight and crooked, what the scale is to weight, what axle and yoke are to the chariot, what bit and bridle are to the horse. Command troops without reward and punishment, and good and bad blur together until no one can be told apart; Apply them without matching merit to reward and fault to penalty, and the reckless win favor while the faithful are cast aside. Either way — whether reward and punishment are abandoned or applied without consistent rule — the result is the same ruin. Lately power has slipped to lower ranks while the court has lost the reins — generals' orders scarcely reach the ranks, and state law cannot bind the commanders; all parties merely indulge one another and let the years slide by. To reward one man of merit is to fear rebellion from those without; To punish one guilty man is to dread unrest among his accomplices. Crimes are hushed up rather than exposed; merit is withheld on suspicion — indulgence has sunk to this level. Those who risk all in loyal service are mocked by their peers; those who lead charges draw hatred from the ranks; those who ruin armies and endanger the realm feel no shame or fear; those who arrive late to save the day congratulate themselves on their cleverness. With neither praise nor blame enforced, rumor and slander swirl without order — though a man wishes to do right, who will speak up for him? The upright and loyal, who ask nothing of others, are the ones who suffer hardship; while cowards who serve private ends and flatter the ranks routinely win favor and promotion. This is what breaks the hearts of men of principle and dissolves the courage of the brave. There are those who fail to hold when the enemy strikes, who offer plans that never succeed; commanders blame insufficient supplies; the quartermasters insist nothing was lacking. With conflicting accounts on the table, the matter ought to be settled — yet the court equivocates and never pursues the truth. The honest swallow their grievances in silence; the deceitful mislead their superiors without a blush. To command troops thus is to abandon accountability entirely!
48
課責虧度，措置乖方，將不得竭其材，卒不得盡其力，屯集雖眾，戰陣莫前。 虜每越境橫行，若涉無人之地； 遞相推倚，無敢誰何，虛張賊勢上聞，則曰兵少不敵。 朝廷莫之省察，惟務征發益師，無裨備禦之功，重增供億之弊。 閭井日耗，征求日繁，以編戶傾家破產之資，兼有司榷鹽稅酒之利，總其所入，半以事邊，制用若斯，可謂財匱於兵眾矣！
With accountability gone and policy misdirected, generals cannot use their full talent nor soldiers their full strength — though armies mass in number, none advance when battle comes. The enemy crosses the border at will, as though marching through empty land; commanders pass the burden to one another, none daring to act; when they must report upward they inflate the enemy's strength and plead that their own numbers are too few. The court never examines the facts, only conscripts more troops — which adds nothing to defense while multiplying the burden of supply. Villages empty day by day, levies multiply — draining registered households to ruin, together with monopolies on salt and taxes on wine, half of all revenue goes to the frontier. Such is the management of funds — the treasury is drained by excessive troop numbers!
49
今四夷之最強盛為中國甚患者，莫大於吐蕃，舉國勝兵之徒，才當中國十數大郡而已。 其於內虞外備，亦與中國不殊，所能寇邊，數則蓋寡。 且又器非犀利，甲不堅完，識迷韜鈐，藝乏趫敏。 動則中國畏其眾而不敢抗，靜則中國憚其強而不敢侵，厥理何哉？ 良以中國之節制多門，蕃醜之統帥專一故也。 夫統帥專則人心不分，人心不分則號令不貳，號令不貳則進退可齊，進退可齊則疾徐如意，疾徐如意則機會靡愆，機會靡愆則氣勢自壯！ 斯乃以少為眾，以弱為強，變化翕辟，在於反掌之內。 是猶臂之使指，心之制形，若所任得人，則何敵之有！ 夫節制多門則人心不一，人心不一則號令不行，號令不行則進退難必，進退難必則疾徐失宜，疾徐失宜則機會不及，機會不及則氣勢自衰！ 斯乃勇廢為尪，眾散為弱，逗撓離析，兆乎戰陣之前。 是猶一國三公，十羊九牧，欲令齊肅，其可得乎？ 開元、天寶之間，控禦西北兩蕃，唯朔方、河西、隴右三節度而已，猶慮權分勢散，或使兼而領之。 中興已來，未遑外討，僑隸四鎮於安定，權附隴右於扶風，所當西北兩蕃，亦朔方、涇原、隴右、河東節度而已，關東戍卒，至則屬焉。 雖委任未盡得人，而措置尚存典制。 自頃逆泚誘涇、隴之眾叛，懷光汙朔方之軍，割裂誅鋤，所余無幾。 而又分朔方之地，建牙擁節者，凡三使焉。 其余鎮軍，數且四十，皆承特詔委寄，各降中貴監臨，人得抗衡，莫相稟屬。 每俟邊書告急，方令計會用兵，既無軍法下臨，唯以客禮相待。 是乃從容拯溺，揖讓救焚，冀無阽危，固亦難矣！ 夫兵，以氣勢為用者也，氣聚則盛，散則消； 勢合則威，析則弱。 今之邊備，勢弱氣消，建軍若斯，可謂力分於將多矣。
Of all the barbarian powers that threaten China today, none is greater than Tibet — yet its entire army scarcely equals the fighting men of a dozen large Chinese prefectures. They face internal worries and external threats much as China does, and the forces they can mount for border raids are relatively few. Their weapons are not keen, their armor not strong, their commanders ignorant of strategy, their soldiers lacking skill and agility. When they move, China fears their numbers and dares not resist; when still, China dreads their strength and dares not attack — why is this? Because China's military command is fragmented among many hands, while the barbarian leader's authority is unified. Unified command means unified purpose; unified purpose means undivided orders; undivided orders mean coordinated movement; coordinated movement means control of pace; control of pace means seizing every opportunity; and seizing opportunity means spirit naturally rises! Thus the few become as many, the weak as strong — transformation at a snap of the fingers. Like the arm directing the fingers, the mind governing the body — appoint the right men and what enemy could stand against you! Fragmented command splits purpose; split purpose means orders fail; failed orders mean movement cannot be coordinated; uncoordinated movement means mistimed action; mistimed action means lost opportunities; and lost opportunities mean spirit collapses! Courage turns to weakness, numbers to scattering — hesitation and fracture appear before battle is even joined. Like three rulers in one kingdom, nine shepherds for ten sheep — can uniformity and discipline come of that? In the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras, defense against the two northwestern powers rested on only three commands — Shuofang, Hexi, and Longyou — and even then the court worried about divided authority, sometimes appointing one man to hold several at once. Since the Restoration, with no capacity for external campaigns, the four western garrisons were lodged at Anding and Longyou temporarily attached to Fufeng — defense against the northwest still fell to Shuofang, Jingyuan, Longyou, and Hedong; eastern garrison troops, when dispatched, reported to them. Appointments were not always ideal, but the institutional framework still held. Lately Zhu Ci lured Jing and Long troops into rebellion; Huai Guang corrupted the Shuofang army — after purges and partition, little remained. Shuofang itself was split among three separate commanders with imperial banners. Other frontier armies, nearly forty in number, each held a special imperial commission with an eunuch overseer — commanders stood as equals, subordinate to none. Only when frontier dispatches report crisis are they summoned to coordinate forces — with no superior military law over them, only mutual courtesy among equals. This is like saving a drowning man without haste, or fighting a fire with polite ceremony — to hope for safety from peril in such fashion is impossible! An army lives by its spirit — gathered it is formidable, scattered it evaporates; united in force it is powerful, divided it is weak. Today's border defense is weak in force and broken in spirit — to organize armies thus is to scatter strength among too many commanders.
50
理戎之要，最在均齊，故軍法無貴賤之差，軍實無多少之異，是將所以同其誌而盡其力也。 如或誘其誌意，勉其藝能，則當閱其材，程其勇，校其勞逸，度其安危，明申練覆優劣之科，以為衣食等級之制。 使能者企及，否者息心，雖有薄厚之殊，而無觖望之釁。 蓋所謂日省月試，餼稟均事，如權量之無情於物，萬人莫不安其分而服其平也。 今者窮邊之地，長鎮之兵，皆百戰傷夷之余，終年勤苦之劇，角其所能則練習，度其所處則孤危，考其服役則勞，察其臨敵則勇。 然衣糧所給，唯止當身，例為妻子所分，常有凍餒之色。 而關東戍卒，歲月踐更，不安危城，不習戎備，怯於應敵，懈於服勞。 然衣糧所頒，厚逾數等，繼以茶藥之饋，益以蔬醬之資。 豐約相形，懸絕斯甚。 又有素非禁旅，本是邊軍，將校詭為媚詞，因請遙隸神策，不離舊所，唯改虛名，其於稟賜之饒，遂有三倍之益。 此儔類所以忿恨，忠良所以憂嗟，疲人所以流亡，經費所以褊匱。 夫事業未異，而給養有殊，人情之所不能甘也，況乎矯佞行而稟賜厚，績藝劣而衣食優，茍未忘懷，能無慍怒！ 不為戎首，則已可嘉，而欲使其協力同心，以攘寇難，雖有韓、白、孫、吳之將，臣知其必不能焉。 養士若斯，可謂怨生於不均矣！
The key to governing troops is equity — hence military law makes no distinction of rank in duty, and provisions no arbitrary difference in amount — this is how commanders align purpose and extract full effort. If one would inspire resolve and cultivate skill, one must assess talent, test courage, weigh hardship against ease and risk against safety — establish clear standards for training review and merit, and from these derive graded provision of food and clothing. Let the able strive upward and the less able accept their place — though provisions differ in degree, none will harbor grievance or cause for mutiny. This is what is meant by daily inspection and monthly review, equal measure in rations — like scales impartial to all objects — so that every man accepts his station and trusts the fairness of the system. Today's far-frontier garrisons are veterans of a hundred battles, men who toil without respite — skilled in arms, isolated in position, exhausted in service, brave before the enemy. Yet their rations cover only themselves, habitually shared with wives and children — they wear the look of cold and hunger. Eastern garrison troops, rotated year by year, never hold dangerous posts, never drill for war — timid in battle, slack in labor. Yet their rations exceed those of frontier men by several grades, supplemented with tea and medicine, vegetables and condiments. Abundance beside want — the disparity is staggering. Some frontier troops, never part of the palace guard, persuade their officers with flattery to nominally join the Shence Army — staying in the same post under a new title, they triple their stipends. Hence resentment among comrades, grief among the loyal, desertion among the worn, and exhaustion of the treasury. Same service, unequal pay — what human nature cannot accept; how much worse when flatterers feast while the skilled go hungry — who could bear it without anger! If they refrain from leading mutiny, that alone is praise-worthy — yet to expect united effort against the enemy, even with commanders like Han Xin, Bai Qi, Sun Wu, or Wu Qi, your subject knows it cannot be done.
