To maintain troops thus is to breed resentment from inequality!
51
凡欲選任將帥，必先考察行能，然後指以所授之方，語以所委之事，令其自揣可否，自陳規模。 須某色甲兵，藉某人參佐，要若干士馬，用若干資糧，某處置軍，某時成績，始終要領，悉俾經綸，於是觀其計謀，校其聲實。 若謂材無足取，言不可行，則當退之於初，不宜貽慮於其後也。 若謂志氣足任，方略可施，則當要之於終，不宜掣肘於其間也。 夫如是，則疑者不使，使者不疑； 勞神於選才，端拱於委任。 既委其事，既足其求，然後可以核其否臧，行其賞罰。 受賞者不以為濫，當罰者無得而辭，付授之柄既專，茍且之心自息。 是以古之遣將帥者，君親推轂而命之曰：「自閫以外，將軍裁之。 」又賜鈇鉞，示令專斷。 故軍容不入國，國容不入軍，將在軍，君命有所不受。 誠謂機宜不可以遠決，號令不可以兩從，未有委任不專，而望其克敵成功者也。 自頃邊軍去就，裁斷多出宸衷，選置戎臣，先求易制，多其部以分其力，輕其任以弱其心，雖有所懲，亦有所失。 遂令分閫責成之義廢，死綏任咎之誌衰，一則聽命，二亦聽命，爽於軍情亦聽命，乖於事宜亦聽命。 若所置將帥，必取於承順無違，則如斯可矣； 若有意平兇靖難，則不可。 夫兩境相接，兩軍相持，事機之來，間不容息，蓄謀而俟，猶恐失之，臨時始謀，固已疏矣。 況乎千里之遠，九重之深，陳述之難明，聽覽之不一，欲其事無遺策，雖聖者亦有所不能焉。 設使謀慮能周，其如權變無及！ 戎虜馳突，迅如風飈，驛書上聞，旬月方報。 守土者以兵寡不敢抗敵，分鎮者以無詔不肯出師，逗留之間，寇已奔逼，托於救援未至，各且閉壘自全。 牧馬屯牛，鞠為椎剽； 穡夫樵婦，罄作俘囚。 雖詔諸鎮發兵，唯以虛聲應援，互相瞻顧，莫敢遮邀，賊既縱掠退歸，此乃陳功告捷。 其敗喪則減百而為一，其捃獲則張百而成千。 將帥既幸於總制在朝，不憂於罪累； 陛下又以為大權由己，不究事情。 用師若斯，可謂機失於遙制矣！
Whenever selecting commanders, one must first examine character and capacity; then specify the territory assigned and the tasks entrusted — let each man judge for himself whether he is fit, and state his own plan. Specify the armor and troops required, the aides needed, the numbers of men and horses, the amount of supplies, where to camp the army and when results are expected — entrust the full plan from start to finish, then assess his strategy and weigh his promises against results. If his talent is deemed inadequate or his plan impracticable, dismiss him at the start — do not let misgivings linger until later. If his resolve is sound and his strategy viable, hold him accountable to the end — do not hamstring him midway. Thus the uncertain are never appointed, and those appointed are never doubted; Exhaust effort in choosing the right men, then sit with hands folded in trust once they are appointed. Once the task is entrusted and resources provided, one may then judge success or failure and administer reward and punishment. The rewarded will not call it excessive; the punished will have no defense — with full authority vested in him, the impulse toward corner-cutting dies of itself. Hence when ancient rulers sent forth their generals, the sovereign would push the chariot wheel and declare: "Beyond the camp gate, the general decides all. " They also bestowed the battle-axe, signifying sole authority to command. Military protocol stayed out of court, court protocol stayed out of camp — in the field, a general need not obey every royal order. Critical decisions cannot be made from afar; orders cannot come from two masters — no commander given divided authority has ever defeated the enemy. Lately, every movement of frontier troops is decided by the throne; military officers are chosen for tractability — their commands multiplied to divide their power, their duties lightened to sap their authority. Some evils are checked, but much is lost. The principle of divided command with full accountability is dead; the will to die at one's post rather than fail is gone — first they obey orders, then they obey orders again, even when military judgment or circumstances demand otherwise. If commanders must be men of blind compliance, this approach suffices; But if the aim is to subdue rebels and repel invaders, it will not do. When two borders meet and two armies face each other, opportunity allows no pause — even prepared plans may be too late; improvisation on the spot is already too late. How much worse across a thousand li, from the depths of the palace — reports are hard to make clear, audiences are inconsistent — to expect flawless strategy from afar exceeds even a sage's power. Even if planning were perfect, there is no time for adaptation! Barbarian raiders strike swift as a gale — by the time a courier reaches court, a month may pass before any reply. Local defenders, too few to fight, dare not resist; neighboring commands, lacking imperial orders, refuse to march — while they delay, the raiders close in; claiming rescue has not arrived, each barricades his fortress and saves himself. Horses and cattle are seized; Farmers and woodcutters become prisoners. Though imperial orders summon troops from every command, they respond with empty gestures — watching one another, none dares intercept the enemy; when the raiders finish plundering and withdraw, they report victory. Defeats are reported as one in a hundred; booty inflated from hundreds to thousands. Commanders, relieved that overall control rests at court, need not fear punishment; Your Majesty, satisfied that supreme authority is yours, does not examine the facts. To wage war thus is to lose every advantage through remote command!
52
理兵而措置乖方，馭將而賞罰虧度，制用而財匱，建兵而力分，養士而怨生，用師而機失，此六者，疆場之蟊賊，軍旅之膏肓也。 蟊賊不除，而但滋之以糞溉，膏肓不療，而唯啖之以滑甘，適足以養其害，速其災，欲求稼穡豐登，膚革充美，固不可得也。
Misdeployment of forces, misjudgment in commanding and rewarding, depleted treasuries, divided military strength, resentful soldiers, lost opportunities in war — these six are pests devouring the frontier and maladies deep in the army's vitals. Leave the pests and only add fertilizer; leave the disease untreated and only offer delicacies — you nourish the harm and hasten disaster. To expect rich harvests and flourishing prosperity is impossible.
53
臣愚謂宜罷諸道將士番替防秋之制，率因舊數而三分之：其一分委本道節度使募少壯願住邊城者以徙焉； 其一分則本道但供衣糧，委關內、河東諸軍州募蕃、漢子弟願傅邊軍者以給焉； 又一分亦令本道但出衣糧，加給應募之人，以資新徙之業。 又令度支散於諸道和市耕牛，兼雇召工人，就諸軍城繕造器具。 募人至者，每家給耕牛一頭，又給田農水火之器，皆令充備。 初到之歲，與家口二人糧，並賜種子，勸之播植，待經一稔，俾自給家。 若有余糧，官為收糴，各酬倍價，務獎營田。 既息踐更征發之煩，且無幸災茍免之弊。 寇至則人自為戰，時至則家自力農。 是乃兵不得不強，食不得不足，與夫倏來忽往，豈可同等而論哉！
Your subject proposes abolishing the rotational autumn-defense system for frontier garrisons and dividing existing force levels into three: one third — let each circuit governor recruit able-bodied men willing to settle on the frontier; One third — the home circuit provides rations while Guannei and Hedong recruit Han and non-Han youth willing to join frontier units; A third portion — the home circuit again supplies rations, with additional grants to recruits to establish new settlements. The Directorate of Revenue should purchase plow oxen across the circuits and hire craftsmen to build equipment at each garrison. Each arriving family should receive a plow ox and full farm implements. In their first year, provide rations for two dependents plus seed and encourage planting — after one harvest they should support themselves. Surplus grain should be bought by the state at double price to encourage frontier agriculture. This would end the burden of rotational service and eliminate the abuse of men who welcome disasters as excuses to shirk duty. When enemies come, every man fights; when seasons turn, every household farms. Thus the army grows strong and provisions abundant — how can this compare with troops that appear and vanish like gusts of wind!
54
臣又謂宜擇文武能臣一人為隴右元帥，應涇、隴、鳳翔、長武城、山南西道等節度管內兵馬，悉以屬焉； 又擇一人為朔方元帥，應鄜坊、邠寧、靈夏等節度管內兵馬，悉以屬焉； 又擇一人為河東元帥，河東、振武等節度管內兵馬，悉以屬焉。 三帥各選臨邊要會之州以為理所，見置節度，有非要者，隨所便近而並之。 唯元帥得置統軍，余並停罷。 其三帥部內太原、鳳翔等府及諸郡戶口稍多者，慎揀良吏以為尹守，外奉師律，內課農桑，俾為軍糧，以壯戎府。 理兵之宜既得，選帥之授既明，然後減奸濫虛浮之費以豐財，定衣糧等級之制以和眾，弘委任之道以宣其用，懸賞罰之典以考其成。 而又慎守中國之所長，謹行當今之所易，則八利可致，六失可除。 如是而戎狄不威懷，疆場不寧謐者，未之有也。 諸侯軌道，庶類服從。 如是而教令不行，天下不理者，亦未之有也。 以陛下之英鑒，民心之思安，四方之小休，兩寇之方靜，加以頻年豐稔，所在積糧，此皆天贊國家，可以立制垂統之時也。 時不久居，事不常兼，已過而追，雖悔無及。 明主者，不以言為罪，不以人廢言，罄陳狂愚，惟所省擇。
Your subject further proposes selecting one capable minister as Longyou commander-in-chief, placing all troops of Jing, Long, Fengxiang, Changwucheng, and Shannan West under his command; One as Shuofang commander, over troops of Fufang, Binning, Lingxia, and related commands; One as Hedong commander, over Hedong, Zhenwu, and related commands. Each of the three commanders should establish headquarters at key frontier prefectures, merging existing commands where convenient and abolishing unnecessary ones. Only the commanders-in-chief may appoint army supervisors; all other such positions should be abolished. In populous prefectures like Taiyuan and Fengxiang within each command, appoint capable magistrates who enforce military discipline outward and promote agriculture inward, building grain reserves to strengthen the frontier. Once forces are properly organized and commanders clearly appointed, cut corrupt and wasteful spending to enrich the treasury, standardize rations to harmonize the ranks, extend full delegation to employ their talents, and establish clear rewards and punishments to measure results. Furthermore, hold fast to China's strengths and pursue reforms within reach — eight benefits will follow and the six failures be removed. If so, the barbarians will not fail to submit in awe, and the frontier will not fail to know peace. Feudal lords will keep to the path; the people will obey. If so, imperial commands will not go unheeded, and the realm will not fail to be governed. With Your Majesty's keen judgment, the people's longing for peace, a brief respite on all sides, the two enemies temporarily quiet, and harvests abundant year after year with grain stored everywhere — heaven favors the state; this is the moment to establish enduring institutions. Favorable times do not linger; advantages rarely coincide — once past, regret avails nothing. A wise sovereign does not punish honest speech or dismiss counsel because of the speaker — your subject lays out these crude thoughts for Your Majesty's consideration alone.
55
德宗極深嘉納，優詔褒獎之。
Emperor Dezong warmly approved and issued an edict commending him.
56
贄在中書，政不便於時者，多所條奏。 德宗雖不能皆可，而心頗重之。 初，竇參既貶郴州，節度使劉士寧餉參絹數千匹。 湖南觀察使李巽與參有隙，具事奏聞，德宗不悅。 會右庶子姜公輔於上前聞奏，稱「竇參嘗語臣云：陛下怒臣未已」，德宗怒，再貶參，竟殺之。 時議雲公輔奏竇參語得之於贄，雲參之死，贄有力焉。 又素惡於公異、於邵，既輔政而逐之，談者亦以為厄。
While Lu Zhi served in the Secretariat, he frequently memorialized on policies that harmed the times. Emperor Dezong could not approve all his proposals, but held him in considerable regard. Earlier, after Dou Can was demoted to Chenzhou, Military Governor Liu Shining sent him several thousand bolts of silk. Hunan Observations Commissioner Li Xun, who bore a grudge against Dou Can, reported the matter in full; Emperor Dezong was displeased. When Right Censor Jiang Gongfu spoke before the throne, saying "Dou Can once told me: 'His Majesty's anger at me is not yet spent'" — the emperor's fury led to a second demotion and ultimately Dou Can's execution. Opinion at the time held that Jiang Gongfu had learned of Dou Can's words from Lu Zhi, and that Lu Zhi had played a part in Dou Can's death. He had long been at odds with Gong Yi and Yu Shao; once in power he drove them out, which critics also regarded as harsh.
57
戶部侍郎、判度支裴延齡，奸宄用事，天下嫉之如仇。 以得幸於天子，無敢言者。 贄獨以身當之，屢於延英面陳其不可，累上疏極言其弊。 延齡日加譖毀。 十年十二月，除太子賓客，罷知政事。 贄性畏慎，及策免私居，朝謁之外，不通賓客，無所過從。 十一年春，旱，邊軍芻粟不給，具事論訴； 延齡言贄與張滂、李充等搖動軍情，語在《延齡傳》。 德宗怒，將誅贄等四人，會諫議大夫陽城等極言論奏，乃貶贄為忠州別駕。
Pei Yanling, Vice Minister of Revenue and acting director of the Directorate of Revenue, was a treacherous schemer in power — the world hated him as an enemy. Because he enjoyed the emperor's favor, no one dared speak against him. Lu Zhi alone stood in his path, repeatedly denouncing him before the throne in the Yanying Hall and submitting memorial after memorial on his abuses. Pei Yanling daily added slanders against him. In the twelfth month of the tenth year, Lu Zhi was appointed Guest of the Heir Apparent and removed from the chancellorship. Lu Zhi was by nature cautious; after his dismissal he stayed home, receiving no visitors beyond required court audiences. In the spring of the eleventh year, drought left frontier troops without fodder, and they petitioned in full detail; Pei Yanling charged that Lu Zhi, Zhang Pang, Li Chong, and others were stirring up military unrest — details are in the 《Biography of Yanling》. Emperor Dezong, enraged, was about to execute all four — but Remonstrance Counselor Yang Cheng and others argued fiercely before the throne, and Lu Zhi was demoted to Assistant Administrator of Zhongzhou.
58
贄初入翰林，特承德宗異顧，歌詩戲狎，朝夕陪遊。 及出居艱阻之中，雖有宰臣，而謀猷參決，多出於贄，故當時目為「內相」。 從幸山南，道途艱險，扈從不及，與帝相失，一夕不至，上喻軍士曰：「得贄者賞千金。 」翌日贄謁見，上喜形顏色，其寵待如此。 既與二吳不協，漸加浸潤，恩禮稍薄； 及通玄敗，上知誣枉，遂復見用。 贄以受人主殊遇，不敢愛身，事有不可，極言無隱。 朋友規之，以為太峻，贄曰：「吾上不負天子，下不負吾所學，不恤其他。 」精於吏事，斟酌決斷，不失錙銖。 嘗以「詞詔所出，中書舍人之職，軍興之際，促迫應務，權令學士代之； 朝野乂寧，合歸職分，其命將相制詔，卻付中書行譴。 」又言「學士私臣，玄宗初令待詔，止於唱和文章而已」。 物議是之。 德宗以贄指斥通微、通玄，故不可其奏。
When Lu Zhi first entered the Hanlin Academy, he enjoyed Emperor Dezong's exceptional favor — singing, composing verses, jesting intimately, accompanying the emperor day and night. During the hardships of the flight to Shanxi, though there were chancellors, most counsel and decisions came from Lu Zhi — contemporaries called him the "inner chancellor." During the journey to Shanxi, the road was perilous; Lu Zhi fell behind the escort and missed the emperor by a night. The emperor told the troops: "Whoever finds Lu Zhi will receive a thousand in gold. " The next day Lu Zhi presented himself — the emperor's joy showed on his face. Such was the favor he received. After falling out with the two Wus, slander gradually took effect and imperial kindness waned; When Tong Xuan's plot failed, the emperor recognized the false accusation and restored Lu Zhi to favor. Having received the sovereign's extraordinary grace, Lu Zhi dared not spare himself — when something was wrong, he spoke without concealment. Friends warned him he was too severe. Lu Zhi replied: "Above, I do not fail the Son of Heaven; below, I do not fail what I have learned — I care for nothing else. " He was skilled in administrative affairs, weighing every decision to the smallest fraction. He once argued: "Proclamations and edicts are properly the duty of Secretariat Drafters; in wartime urgency it was permitted to let academicians stand in temporarily; Now that court and country are at peace, those duties should revert — appointments of generals and chancellors and formal edicts should return to the Secretariat. " He also said: "Academicians are private retainers — Emperor Xuanzong initially had them wait on edicts merely to compose poetry in reply." Public opinion agreed with him. Emperor Dezong rejected his memorial because it implicitly condemned Tong Wei and Tong Xuan.
59
贄在忠州十年，常閉關靜處，人不識其面，復避謗，不著書。 家居瘴鄉，人多癘疫，乃抄撮方書，為《陸氏集驗方》五十卷，行於代。 初，贄秉政，貶駕部員外郎李吉甫為明州長史，量移忠州刺史。 贄在忠州，與吉甫相遇，昆弟、門人鹹為贄憂，而吉甫忻然厚禮，都不銜前事，以宰相禮事之，猶恐其未信不安，日與贄相狎，若平生交契者。 贄初猶慚懼，後乃深交。 時論以吉甫為長者。 後有薛延者，代吉甫為刺史，延朝辭日，德宗令宣旨慰安。 而韋臯累上表請以贄代己。 順宗即位，與陽城、鄭余慶同詔征還。 詔未至而贄卒，時年五十二，贈兵部尚書，謚曰宣。
Lu Zhi spent ten years in Zhongzhou behind closed doors — so reclusive that people did not know his face; fearing slander, he wrote no books. Living in a malarial region where pestilence was common, he compiled medical formulas into fifty volumes titled 《Lu's Collected Verified Formulas》, which circulated in his age. Earlier, while Lu Zhi held power, he had demoted Li Jiyuan, Vice Director of the Transport Office, to chief administrator of Mingzhou, later transferred to prefect of Zhongzhou. When Lu Zhi was in Zhongzhou and met Li Jiyuan, Lu's brothers, disciples, and students all feared for him — but Li Jiyuan received him warmly, bore no grudge, treated him with the courtesy owed a chancellor, and daily kept close company as if they had been friends all along. At first Lu Zhi was ashamed and afraid; afterward they became close friends. Contemporary opinion hailed Li Jiyuan as a man of magnanimity. Later Xue Yan succeeded Li Jiyuan as prefect; on the day Xue took leave at court, Emperor Dezong had comforting words conveyed to Lu Zhi. Meanwhile Wei Gao repeatedly memorialized asking that Lu Zhi replace him. When Emperor Shunzong ascended, Lu Zhi was summoned back by edict along with Yang Cheng and Zheng Yuqing. Before the edict arrived, Lu Zhi died at fifty-two — posthumously honored as Minister of War, posthumous name Xuan.
60
子簡禮，登進士第，累辟使府。
His son Jianli passed the jinshi examination and was repeatedly invited to serve in provincial staffs.
61
史臣曰：近代論陸宣公，比漢之賈誼，而高邁之行，剛正之節，經國成務之要，激切仗義之心，初蒙天子重知，末塗淪躓，皆相類也。 而誼止中大夫，贄及臺鉉，不為不遇矣。 昔公孫鞅挾三策說秦王，淳于髡以隱語見齊君，從古以還，正言不易。 昔周昭戒急論議，正為此也。 贄居珥筆之列，調飪之地，欲以片心除眾弊，獨手遏群邪，君上不亮其誠，群小共攻其短，欲無放逐，其可得乎！ 《詩》稱「其維哲人，告之話言」，又有「誨爾」、「聽我」之恨，此皆賢人君子，嘆言不見用也。 故堯咨禹拜，千載一時，攜手提耳，豈容易哉！
The historian writes: In recent times Lu Xuangong has been compared to Jia Yi of Han — in lofty conduct, upright integrity, mastery of statecraft, and fierce devotion to righteousness; first enjoying the emperor's deep trust, then suffering ruin at the end — they are alike in all this. Yet Jia Yi reached only Grand Master of the Palace, while Lu Zhi attained the chancellorship — he was hardly ill-treated. Long ago Gongsun Yang brought three plans to the King of Qin; Chunyu Kun won audience with the King of Qi through riddles — from antiquity onward, honest speech has never been easy. Duke Zhao of Zhou warned against hasty debate — precisely for this reason. Lu Zhi stood among the draftsmen and stewards of counsel, seeking with his single heart to remove countless abuses and alone hold back the multitude of villains — the sovereign did not credit his sincerity, petty men together attacked his faults — how could exile have been avoided! The Book of Odes praises the wise ruler who heeds frank counsel, and mourns the teacher whose words go unheeded—such is the lament of every worthy man whose advice is ignored. When Yao sought counsel and Yu received it, that was a bond rare in a thousand years—hand in hand, whispering guidance. Such trust is not easily won!
62
贊曰：良臣悟主，我有嘉猷。 多僻之君，為善不周。 忠言救失，啟沃曰讎。 勿貽天問，蒼昊悠悠。
Eulogy: The worthy minister enlightens his sovereign—I have a plan that will avail. The perverse ruler practices virtue only in part. Loyal counsel repairs error, yet frank guidance is treated as a foe. Lest Heaven itself pose the question—under the endless sky.
